item.title: A Minimal Hamiltonian Predicts Genome Architecture across Resolutions and Cell Types
item.description:
Abstract
The three-dimensional organization of the genome underlies essential regulatory processes and is commonly inferred from two-dimensional Hi-C contact maps. Although higher-resolution data sets reveal increasingly rich structural features, training polymer models at fine genomic resolutions remains computationally demanding and often unstable. Here, we show that the Minimal Chromatin Model (MiChroM) learns a Hamiltonian whose underlying energetic principles remain remarkably consistent from 100 kb down to 10 kb resolution. While compartment-driven interactions are largely preserved across scales, refinement of the effective potential describing genomic-distance-dependent chromatin compaction, the ideal chromosome potential, progressively resolves finer structural features, including local contact heterogeneity and topologically associating domains, without altering the global folding framework. We further introduce an efficient sliced-map training strategy that optimizes the key energetic terms using only a representative subset of the Hi-C matrix, enabling rapid and stable construction of high-resolution models. At a given resolution, the learned Hamiltonian accurately predicts chromatin organization across the genome and diverse cell types without additional chromosome- or cell-type-specific optimization. Across resolutions, the conserved interaction hierarchy provides a transferable initialization, whereas numerical parameter values require resolution-specific calibration. These results demonstrate that chromosome architecture can be understood as the interplay between a universal physical Hamiltonian and cell-type-specific compartment annotations, providing a practical and physically interpretable framework for predictive modeling of genome organization.

item.title: ModBind dG as a Physics-Based Oracle: Training Drug Discovery AI Models with Little or No Experimental Data
item.description:
Abstract
AI models of drug–target binding affinity are limited by the scarcity of experimental data, particularly for novel or understudied targets. Here, we show that ModBinddG, a rapid molecular-simulation-based method for predicting absolute binding free energies, can serve as a physics-based oracle that generates synthetic affinity data accurate enough to train predictive AI models with little or no experimental data. First, we demonstrate across 16 diverse chemical series and 16 X-ray structures, with diverse protein conformations and binding modes, that ModBinddG predicts absolute binding free energies with a mean unsigned error of approximately 1 kcal/mol without per-series calibration. We then show that a target-specific AI model trained solely on ModBinddG predictions, using no experimental labels, accurately ranks the held-out experimental affinities. Extending this idea to general drug–target interaction (DTI) models, we introduce ModBindAL, an active-learning framework that uses ModBinddG as the oracle to iteratively augment a general DTI model (DeepConvDTI). Across three additional kinase targets, synthetic data augmentation improved test-set Pearson correlation for all three targets tested. Because two distinct AI architectures both benefit from the ModBinddG oracle, the accuracy of the synthetic data rather than any specific model appears to drive the improvement. In the course of this work, we identified and corrected substantial train/test contamination and a missing-negative-example issue in the CARA benchmark, establishing a fairer baseline for evaluation. Together, these results indicate that high-quality synthetic absolute binding affinity data from a physics-based oracle can build and improve AI models of drug–target affinity with minimal experimental data, with direct implications for all stages of early drug discovery.

item.title: A Multiplexed Sampling Strategy for Generating Diverse Protein Conformations with Generative Deep Networks: A General Framework Illustrated with Aβ42
item.description:
Abstract
This paper introduces a novel generative framework, ProFormX, that combines variational autoencoding with GAN-style generation from noise to synthesize diverse and stable protein conformations, specifically focusing on Amyloid-β1–42 (Aβ42). Traditional methods struggle with Aβ42’s conformational flexibility and aggregation tendencies. ProFormX leverages a new sampling technique within its latent space to generate energetically stable and physically valid conformations, overcoming issues like mode collapse and poor sample diversity. The model learns from the intrinsic disorder of Aβ42 dynamics and explores its conformational space to produce novel structures not seen in the training dataset. Extensive computational experiments demonstrate ProFormX’s efficiency in generating novel Aβ42 structures, providing insights into its conformational landscape, and identifying key characteristics associated with Aβ42 aggregation, which may provide candidate structures for future studies of neurodegenerative diseases. The study also highlights the model’s ability to capture biologically important structures, including specific hairpin formations and the interplay between salt bridges and hydrophobic packing in forming toxic conformations.

item.title: Conformer Handling in Machine-Learned 31 P NMR Prediction: How Many, How Weighted, and When It Matters
item.description:
Abstract
Conformer ensembles improve machine-learned 31P NMR shift prediction, but the improvement is unevenly distributed across the workflow; aggregating predictions over an ensemble at inference time gains around 0.23 ppm against a 10.5 ppm baseline, whereas training on a conformer ensemble rather than a single structure gains about four times more. This paper examines the conditions under which conformers are worth generating and how many are needed by statistically evaluating experimental results on the Ilm-NMR-P31 data set. Both effects saturate at five conformers per molecule, recovering 94% of the training time benefit and 82% of the inference time benefit, and tripling the training set beyond that point yields nothing measurable, so the benefit does not follow from training set size alone. On unrefined GFN2-xTB geometries of the same conformers, the training time effect, the inference time effect of models trained on all conformers, and their saturation at five conformers are reproduced. For models trained on conformer ensembles, neither the weighting of the conformers nor their selection matters in practice; conformers drawn at random and averaged equally perform as well as energy-ranked, Boltzmann-weighted ensembles, thus allowing the expensive frequency analysis to be skipped. No significant difference in the usefulness of conformers was detected across phosphorus chemistry or local flexibility, although the statistical power of the smaller P(III) subgroups was limited. At a fixed training-set size, however, rows spent on previously unrepresented molecules are worth considerably more than rows spent on further geometries of molecules already present, so broadening the set of molecules is the better investment where conformer generation is the limiting cost.

item.title: LICA: A Multiview Relation-Aware Equivariant Graph Neural Network with Interfacial Atomic-Pair Attention for Protein–Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Accurate prediction of protein–ligand binding affinity is foundational in structure-based drug design, yet existing 3D graph models often mix heterogeneous chemical relations and dilute sparse interfacial signals through global pooling. We present LICA, a relation-aware equivariant graph neural network that explicitly distinguishes covalent, spatial, and interfacial contacts on a unified 3D graph. A multiview readout extracts complementary information from the ligand, the pocket, and explicit interfacial atom pairs. Trained under a leakage-controlled Tanimoto split and tested independently on CASF-2016, LICA shows that prediction errors concentrate in sparsely sampled extreme-affinity regions, exhibiting a regression-to-the-mean extrapolation bottleneck. Ablation studies demonstrate that the explicit interfacial atom-pair attention provides a meaningful geometric inductive bias rather than merely adding parameters. This bias is particularly effective for spatially directional interactions, such as cation−π contacts. Using structural annotations as a reference, we further show that the learned interface attention highly overlaps with true short-range contacts. However, case studies reveal that these attention weights serve as a qualitative map of physical interactions and should not be interpreted as a quantitative decomposition of binding free energy. Overall, explicit interface pairing improves affinity regression while yielding a chemically verifiable representation of protein–ligand interactions.

item.title: RMG-Py v4: 17 Years of Open-Source Reaction Mechanism Generation
item.description:
Abstract
Kinetic modeling describes reacting chemical systems through networks of elementary reactions and their associated rate parameters. Reaction Mechanism Generator (RMG-Py) automates the construction of these networks by simulating reaction fluxes to identify dominant chemical pathways in silico. RMG-Py v4.0.0 marks 17 years of open-source reaction mechanism generation, introducing substantial improvements in performance, usability, and chemical scope. Benchmarks demonstrate higher throughput in constructing combustion models relative to prior versions, alongside streamlined installation via Docker and binary distributions. Key new capabilities include automated library selection, improved species selection algorithms, integration with the Julia-based ReactionMechanismSimulator.jl for simulating arbitrary reactor configurations, and PySIDT-based property estimators. Heterogeneous catalysis support is improved by the addition of new adsorbate thermophysical property data, new reaction families, resonance templates of surface-bound species, and uncertainty quantification for parameter sensitivity analysis. The release also extends RMG-Py into new chemical domains, including electrochemical mechanisms for battery and CO2RR applications, and an automated fragment-based modeling framework for the pyrolysis of large molecules. Together, these advances improve new users’ experience, expand the range of tractable systems, and maintain RMG-Py at the forefront of computational kinetic modeling.

item.title: miRNA–mRNA Binding Prediction Model Using Unknown and Experimentally Nondetected Interaction Data
item.description:
Abstract
MicroRNA (miRNA)– messenger RNA (mRNA) interactions inhibit gene expression, including the expression of disease-associated genes, and therefore have broad applications in drug discovery and therapeutics; however, experimental identification is challenging owing to the vast number of possible combinations and the high cost of experimentation. In this study, we developed a method for predicting miRNA–mRNA interactions using pseudonegative sampling and ensemble learning. Unlabeled miRNA–mRNA pairs were randomly sampled as pseudonegative training data, and 100 LightGBM classifiers were constructed to reduce dependence on particular training data selections. Using 248 experimentally nondetected interaction pairs collected through a literature review, we evaluated the ensemble binding scores and explored the usefulness of different sequence-derived explanatory variables. The combination of screening, k-mer first–last distance, and CKSNAP showed better discrimination between experimentally confirmed binding pairs and nonbinding pairs than the other feature combinations examined in this exploratory analysis. These findings suggest that pseudonegative sampling-based ensemble learning provides a useful framework for investigating miRNA–mRNA interactions.

item.title: Chemical Language Models for Prediction of Radiolytic Transformation Products from Molecular Structure
item.description:
Abstract
Assessing the fate of organic compounds under ionizing radiation requires knowing which degradation products form, yet identifying them experimentally is slow and costly. We ask how well machine-learning models can generate those products from a parent compound’s structure alone. Because reported product distributions depend on irradiation conditions that studies record inconsistently, we target a condition-agnostic screening task: recovering the set of products reported for a parent under any condition. We compile a curated benchmark of 446 experimentally reported reactant–product pairs across 128 parent compounds from the primary radiolysis and photolysis literature, and cast prediction as one-to-many SMILES generation under reagent-level repeated cross-validation. GT4SD achieved the highest mean Hit@10 among the models evaluated under shared cross-validation, recovering at least one reported product for 59.4% of parent compounds, compared with 41.1% for nearest-neighbor retrieval. These results demonstrate the potential of chemistry-pretrained language models to generate radiolytic transformation-product candidates for experimental follow-up. Open-weight models further enable local deployment and control over molecular data, supporting their practical use in radiolysis research.

item.title: Multiscale Topological Transcriptomic Analysis for Alzheimer’s Disease Drug Repurposing
item.description:
Abstract
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a complex neurodegenerative disorder driven by multifactorial molecular mechanisms, which severely limit the efficacy of current therapeutic interventions. To accelerate the discovery of novel treatments, we propose a comprehensive computational framework integrating transcriptomic analysis, topological network characterization, machine learning (ML), and structure-based evaluation. By analyzing eight independent AD transcriptomic datasets, we constructed protein–protein interaction networks and implemented a multiscale topological differentiation strategy based on persistent homology and persistent spectral theory. This approach quantified the topological importance of each gene, prioritizing 67 nonredundant key genes. To bridge target identification with drug screening, we mapped these genes to the ChEMBL database, yielding 4,493 bioactivity records across five primary targets. We evaluated three ML algorithms across diverse molecular representations, including two natural language processing-derived molecular embeddings and a conventional molecular fingerprint. Deploying these predictive models for large-scale virtual screening of the DrugBank database yielded several promising repurposing candidates. Subsequent molecular docking against the target proteins GLP1R and CASP1 generated predicted binding poses for selected compounds. Physicochemical profiling identified differences relevant to their further assessment, although these computational results do not establish binding stability, pharmacokinetic suitability, or safety. This study not only identifies viable therapeutic candidates for AD but also provides a scalable, generalizable pipeline for target prioritization and drug discovery applicable to other complex human diseases.

item.title: MolCodon: A Codon-Based Molecular Language for Interpretable Structural Representation and Similarity Search
item.description:
Abstract
Molecular representation determines which aspects of chemical structure can be learned, compared, and interpreted in computational drug discovery. Existing encodings typically emphasize either compact string description, as in SMILES and SELFIES, or efficient similarity search, as in circular fingerprints. Although canonical SMILES already provides a deterministic string, its tokens are variable in width and carry no fixed chemical role. No existing representation simultaneously offers fixed-width, role-assigned tokenization, graph-level interpretability, pharmacophore annotation, and high-fidelity molecular reconstruction. Here, we introduce MolCodon, a codon-based molecular language that represents small molecules as deterministic sequences of fixed-width three-character tokens over a five-symbol alphabet, C, N, O, S, and X. Inspired by the triplet organization of the genetic code, MolCodon assigns chemically defined codon families to atoms, bonds, ring and branch topology, fused-ring references, pharmacophore features, bond mobility, charge, and stereochemistry. A deterministic graph traversal with ring-contiguity preservation produces sequences in which chemically meaningful substructures remain locally organized and traceable to the underlying molecular graph. Across approximately 2.9 million molecules from six commercial screening libraries, MolCodon achieved 98.93% InChIKey-level round-trip fidelity, supporting its use as a high-fidelity sequence representation for drug-like compounds. Across ten QSAR tasks, MolCodon-derived sparse sequence and trace features showed statistically supported advantages over the SMILES and SELFIES-based representations in most data sets while achieving competitive performance with classical fingerprints. These findings are supported by five repeated cross-validation and Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons. As an application of the representation, the MolCodon similarity engine decomposes molecular similarity into ring topology, branch context, attachment architecture, and pharmacophore correspondence, enabling interpretable scaffold-hopping searches. In a PARP1 virtual screening case study, MolCodon retrieved scaffold-diverse candidates using a known PARP-1 inhibitor Olaparib as the template compound. Together, these results establish MolCodon as a new molecular representation paradigm that transforms chemical graphs into high-fidelity, interpretable, and alignment-compatible codon sequences, opening a direct path for bioinformatics-inspired analysis of small-molecule chemical space. The MolCodon encoder, decoder, and similarity engine are freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/DurdagiLab/MolCodon.

item.title: Atom-Wise Allocation of Message-Passing Scale for Molecular Property Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Molecular properties depend on chemical structure at different ranges, from local polar groups governing solvation to extended substructures shaping bioactivity, yet graph neural networks usually fix one propagation scale for every atom. We present PRISM (Per-atom Routing over Intermediate States of Message Passing), in which each atom’s encoded features produce a bounded scalar that positions a unimodal distribution over retained message-passing states and matching circular-fingerprint radii. Because one coordinate translates the whole profile, allocated depth responds to the routing scalar in closed form: at fixed temperature it is nondecreasing, its sensitivity scales with the profile variance, and it saturates in the clipped regions. Beyond providing closed-form analyzability, this constrained one-parameter profile matches or significantly outperforms parameter-matched, unconstrained node-wise gates and Jumping Knowledge attention. Under scaffold partitions with equal tuning budgets against eight graph, fingerprint, and geometric baselines, PRISM trained from scratch without three-dimensional coordinates achieves the lowest mean error on aqueous solubility and hydration free energy and strong accuracy on BACE and BBBP. As a general layer-combination rule, PRISM transfers directly to GCN, GIN, and GAT backbones, reducing hydration free energy error by up to 29% relative to last-layer readout. Applied to a pretrained GIN, it improves on last-layer readout on four of six endpoints and gives the lowest lipophilicity error overall. In trained models, allocated depth differs systematically between atom types in a task-dependent way, and permuting profiles among a molecule’s atoms raises prediction error on several endpoints, so the rule acts as a learned counterpart of atom typing.

item.title: Allosteric Control and Glycan Shielding Adaptations in the SARS-CoV-2 Spike from Early to Peak Virulence
item.description:
Abstract
The SARS-CoV-2 Spike glycoprotein is central to viral infectivity and immune evasion, making it a key target for vaccine and therapeutic design. This trimeric peplomer undergoes dynamic conformational changes, particularly in its Receptor Binding Domain (RBD), which transitions between closed (down) and ACE2-accessible (up) states relative to the rest of the protein, to facilitate host cell entry. Structural understanding of such critical interdomain motions, as well as epitope exposure quantification, is essential for obtaining an effective biochemical handle over this protein and, in turn, exploiting it toward improved immunogen development. Focusing on the early circulating D614G form and the later emerging Delta (B.1.617.2) variant with higher virulence, we performed large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of the soluble form of the Spike in both “down” and “up” conformations of the RBD. Guided by differences in domain-scale fluctuations, we constructed targeted reaction coordinates capturing NTD and RBD rotations and tilting motions, enabling variant-specific structural distinctions to be quantitatively extracted. Conformational landscape mapping and principal component analysis (PCA) reveal a previously uncharacterized dynamic coupling between the NTD and RBD, wherein tilting motions of the NTD are coupled to RBD gating on the neighboring protomer. While several elements of this interdomain coupling are conserved, the Delta variant exhibits a more constrained and functionally optimized RBD-up conformation that favors ACE2 engagement. Concurrently, Delta-specific mutations restructure NTD-local glycans to enhance shielding of the immunogenic supersite, diminishing neutralizing antibody accessibility. Finally, the D950N substitution at the heptad repeat HR1 helix reshapes long-range interactions and alters bending/twisting dynamics of the Spike stalk, likely contributing to both fusion efficiency and immune evasion. Together, these simulations uncover chemically encoded strategies of variant adaptation─through long-range allostery, glycan repositioning, and conformational bias─that shape Spike structure and function. These biochemical and structural insights offer valuable guidance for rational vaccine and therapeutic design against SARS-CoV-2 and emerging variants.

item.title: Shake It Off: Abl Kinase Regulatory Domain Dynamics Explain Conformational Changes upon Activation
item.description:
Abstract
Abl kinase is a major molecular target for chronic myeloid leukemia therapy. Its activity is tightly controlled by its regulatory module, composed of the SH3 and SH2 domains and the SH2–kinase linker. Although the assembled autoinhibited and extended active conformations have been structurally characterized, the molecular pathway connecting these states remains poorly understood. Simulations initiated from the end point structures failed to sample the complete transition, even when Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) was employed to enhance conformational sampling. To overcome this limitation, we combined multiscale modeling with extensive molecular dynamics simulations and Markov state modeling to reconstruct the Abl disassembly pathway. The resulting kinetic landscape revealed two coupled conformational equilibria: a faster exchange between the canonical assembled state and an intermediate ensemble that captures the initial rotation of the regulatory module, and a slower transition toward the extended state, characterized by migration of the regulatory module atop the kinase domain N-lobe. The assembled ensemble is favored (∼88% of the equilibrium population), with the canonical autoinhibited arrangement alone accounting for approximately 60%, while early disassembly disrupts the E98–K294 and SH3–linker interactions and releases Y226 from its protective interactions, while Y70 remains accessible through the intrinsic dynamics of the SH3 domain. By revealing how these phosphorylation-sensitive residues become accessible during the earliest stages of disassembly, our model provides a mechanistic framework for Abl activation and identifies regulatory interfaces as potential targets for allosteric stabilization of the autoinhibited state.

item.title: Comment on “Hybrid Graph–Machine Learning Framework for Accurate and Interpretable Band Gap Prediction”
item.description:
Abstract
Aydin et al. reported R2 = 0.921 for band gap prediction using hybrid graph neural networks. Reproduction shows this performance is inflated by data leakage from post-DFT proxies (is_metal, is_gap_direct) and embedding contamination. Controlled ablations reveal a genuine GNN gain of 0.08–0.11 in R2, while leakage contributes ∼0.06, lowering honest performance to 0.82–0.86 R2 (MAE 0.28–0.30 eV).

item.title: DeepChem-DEL: An Open-Source Framework for Reproducible DEL Modeling and Benchmarking
item.description:
Abstract
DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) allow screening of extremely large chemical spaces by tagging compounds with DNA barcodes. Machine learning (ML) techniques have enabled the extraction of meaningful chemical patterns from noisy, target-specific DEL binding data. However, existing tools for DEL machine learning (DEL-ML) remain fragmented, which limits systematic construction and reproducibility of modeling pipelines. Moreover, this fragmentation hinders integration of new models, such as chemical foundation models, into DEL workflows alongside classical approaches. To address these challenges in DEL modeling, we introduce DeepChem-DEL, an open-source suite of reproducible ML workflows for DEL modeling built on the DeepChem ecosystem. DeepChem-DEL integrates (i) a configurable denoising pipeline with (ii) modular DeepChem workflows for enrichment prediction, hit identification, and benchmarking across diverse model classes, including chemical foundation models enabled through extensions to the open-source ChemBERTa-3 framework. We evaluate DeepChem-DEL on the KinDEL and BELKA data sets, reproducing key baselines and enabling direct comparison across model classes. Our experiments demonstrate that leveraging chemical foundation models yields performance competitive with, and in several cases exceeding, previously explored approaches such as graph convolutional networks and random forest models. Together, these results demonstrate that DeepChem-DEL is a scalable and extensible platform for DEL-ML, while highlighting the potential of chemical foundation models for improved DEL modeling and prioritization.

item.title: PolymerFFKit: Bridging Polymer Chemistry and Simulation-Ready Inputs through Traceable Force-Field and Topology Generation
item.description:
Abstract
Polymer molecular dynamics (MD) input preparation often separates experimental characterization, resolution mapping, bonded-parameter fitting, topology construction, and engine-specific file writing into weakly connected steps. PolymerFFKit is a cross-platform application that connects these steps for polymer force-field assembly and topology generation. It supports all-atom (AA), united-atom (UA), and coarse-grained (CG) representations; extracts bonded-coordinate statistics; obtains potential-of-mean-force (PMF) profiles by Boltzmann inversion; records fitting-domain choices; builds sequence-controlled polymer topologies; and exports GROMACS- and LAMMPS-oriented input files. PolymerFFKit v1.0.0 is available at https://tongshi0305-cpu.github.io/. Its main contribution is traceable preparation: mapping rules, fitted domains, random seeds, sequence definitions, and writer outputs remain part of the preparation record. In a hydroxyl-terminated polybutadiene (HTPB) case study, gel permeation chromatography (GPC), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) measurements defined sample-specific molar-mass and microstructure descriptors, while differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) provided an independent glass transition temperature (Tg). PolymerFFKit-derived coarse-grained simulations preserved the experimental Tg ranking across three independent runs for each sample. The above results demonstrate that PolymerFFKit establishes a high-quality, standardized workflow for polymer simulation, bridging experimental synthesis and characterization with the prediction of polymer properties.

item.title: BALLROOM A and S–A Benchmark Created Automatically from Structurally Resolved Pockets with Homogeneously Measured Affinities/Series
item.description:
Abstract
Computational methods for virtual screening and lead optimization are benchmarked on specifically designed data sets to predict compound potency. Here we present a workflow and two resulting new benchmark data sets, BALLROOM A and BALLROOM S, from combining PDB and ChEMBL data. Due to high data quality standards, the formation of molecule pairs measured under the same conditions only, and avoiding pairs with close to equal potency, we achieve a reliable data collection for physics-based bioactivity prediction based on protein–ligand complex structures. When testing state-of-the-art scoring functions for docking, no classical method statistically outperforms a simple molecular-weight-based prediction, consistent with previous studies such as D3R. While challenging for physics-based methods, the prediction task can be easily addressed by simple nearest-neigbor scorers showing that the benchmark cannot be used for machine learing based scoring functions due to significant train-test inference.

item.title: Prospective Execution of a Generative Peptide Design Workflow at the Keap1–Nrf2 Interface
item.description:
Abstract
Deep-learning tools for peptide design and structure prediction are increasingly combined into screening workflows, but at the Keap1–Nrf2 interface such work has rarely progressed beyond computational characterization. We report a case study in which an initial-round workflow built from publicly available components─ProteinMPNN, Chai-1, PLIP, and HADDOCK3─was fixed before any experimental data were obtained and its complete prioritized output was carried to synthesis and measurement: 530,299 unique sequences from seven Nrf2-derived backbones were reduced to 5,118 by sequence filtering and to 28 by structure-based filtering, and all 28 were synthesized and assayed alongside 16 analogues and the native Nrf2 12-mer, giving 45 measured peptides. One design, a 12-mer carrying an ENGE variant of the ETGE motif, inhibited the interaction with an apparent IC50 of 120 nM under the assay conditions used, whereas the 14 resampled analogues satisfying the same structural criteria showed low inhibition, indicating that within this workflow the structure-based steps acted as filters for structural plausibility rather than as predictors of activity. Because the set was measured in full and the intermediate sequence sets were retained, we also report how the composition of the surviving population changed across the cascade; the original workflow data are released.

item.title: ezABFE: An Easy-to-Use Workflow for Absolute Binding Free Energy Calculations
item.description:
Abstract
Absolute binding free energy (ABFE) calculations can evaluate chemically diverse ligands, but their complex workflows remain challenging for nonexpert users and prone to errors. Here, we present ezABFE, an easy-to-use Python workflow for automated ABFE calculations within the AMBER ecosystem. ezABFE minimizes manual intervention in system preparation, representative-structure selection, Boresch restraint atom selection, simulation setup, free-energy estimation, and graphical analysis. The workflow employs both MBAR and TI for alchemical free-energy estimation and additionally provides MM-GBSA and optional MM-PBSA end-point calculations. Benchmarking across T4 lysozyme L99A, BRD4(1), CDK8, and the theophylline-binding RNA aptamer shows good overall agreement with experimentally derived binding free energies and comparable performance of MBAR and TI. Additional tests demonstrate that appropriate Boresch restraint atom selection is important for simulation stability and binding free-energy accuracy, and that ligand partial-charge models and the HMR/4 fs simulation protocol can influence calculated affinities, although the limited comparisons do not support general conclusions regarding either factor. The computationally inexpensive end-point methods also retain practical value for ligand ranking. Overall, ezABFE provides an accessible, automated workflow for reproducible ABFE calculations with improved throughput across diverse receptor systems, including nucleic acid receptors.

item.title: ScentOR: Semantic-Only Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation for Odorant Receptor Deorphanization
item.description:
Abstract
Predicting interactions between odorant ligands and odorant receptor (OR) proteins is hindered by the scarcity of experimental structures and the wide sequence divergence within the OR family. We introduce ScentOR (Semantic Chemical Encoder via Neural Transfer for Odorant Receptors), a heterogeneous knowledge distillation framework that transfers the predictive distributions of a gradient boosting (GB) teacher into a neural network (NN) student using only one-dimensional (1D) semantic representations, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.954 and a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.602 on the curated M2OR data set of 39,723 odorant ligand-OR protein pairs, matching the current best-performing model while reducing the run-to-run standard deviation approximately 3-fold. A systematic comparison of eight scenarios shows that statically predicted three-dimensional (3D) topologies, encoded as geometry alone and at the accuracy currently attainable for ORs, add no complementary value: student models assign them near-zero importance, and the small gain they produce without distillation does not survive it. We further characterize what post hoc attribution reports for a model of this design, showing that integrated gradients (IG) and in silico alanine mutagenesis concentrate on the family-conserved DRY motif arginine yet carry no pair-specific information, even though pair-specific interaction dominates the predictions.

item.title: Predicting Mutation-Induced Alterations in Protein Solubility Using an Attention-Guided Multimodal Learning Method
item.description:
Abstract
Protein solubility plays a crucial role in recombinant protein production and protein developability. However, the vast mutational space makes exhaustive experimental screening costly and time-consuming, motivating computational approaches to prioritize candidate mutations. Predicting mutation-induced solubility changes remains challenging because mutation effects are associated with both the sequence context and the local three-dimensional physicochemical environment. Although multimodal models can integrate complementary sequence- and structure-related representations, the predictive contribution and biological meaning of individual architectural components cannot be inferred directly from the learned fusion behavior. Herein, we developed AttenSol, an attention-guided multimodal framework that integrates mutation-sensitive sequence representations with topology-informed graph processing through a learned fusion mechanism. On the held-out benchmark, AttenSol achieved a balanced accuracy of 52.8%. Control experiments showed that AttenSol did not exhibit a statistically significant balanced accuracy (BACC) advantage over the evaluated direct-fusion and topology-informed GCN comparators, while the learned fusion gate showed a strong but nearly constant preference for the graph-processed branch. Fixed-gate and topology-perturbation analyses indicated that this weighting should not be interpreted as evidence of structural information dominance or strong sample-adaptive routing. Forward–reverse analysis showed strong directional consistency when reverse-mutation augmentation was used, whereas matched retraining without this augmentation reversed the correlation pattern and substantially increased the zero-sum error. Cross-data set evaluation on SoluProtMutDB yielded a BACC of 0.397, revealing a substantial performance reduction under data set and domain shift. Together, these results position AttenSol as a multimodal framework for mutation effect prediction and computational prioritization while emphasizing the need for explicit control analyses when interpreting learned fusion behavior.

item.title: TH-CADD: An Integrated High-Performance Computing Platform for Large-Scale Computer-Aided Drug Discovery
item.description:
Abstract
The growing scale of chemical libraries and the increasing complexity of biological targets have made high-throughput computer-aided drug design (CADD) an essential component of modern drug discovery. Here, we present TH-CADD, a high-performance computer-aided drug discovery platform built on the New Generation Tianhe supercomputer. TH-CADD integrates target preparation and analysis, ligand preparation, similarity search, molecular docking, postdocking analysis, and molecular dynamics simulation into a unified computational framework. A Django-Vue architecture deployed on Tianhe Cloud provides web-based access to high-performance computing (HPC) resources through scheduler-controlled execution. By organizing established CADD tools into a coherent workflow, TH-CADD supports accessible, traceable, and scalable computational drug discovery. The platform supports multiple molecular input formats, automated preprocessing, large-scale screening, and molecular dynamics evaluation of selected protein–ligand complexes. TH-CADD’s contribution lies in the system-level integration, automated job management, and scalable execution of established computational methods on the New Generation Tianhe supercomputer, together with a unified workflow view that supports direct cross-module reuse of compatible task outputs.

item.title: HiFiPL-Bench: A Fidelity-First and Bias-Aware Benchmark for Diagnosing Protein–Ligand Scoring Functions
item.description:
Abstract
Accurate prediction of protein–ligand binding affinities is fundamental to structure-based drug design, yet existing benchmarks are often limited by outdated structural coverage, uncertain local structural fidelity, and physicochemical or protocol-dependent bias. Here, we present HiFiPL-Bench, a fidelity-first and bias-aware benchmark curated from RCSB PDB and BindingDB through hierarchical filtering, manual electron-density validation, affinity verification, and property-matched decoy generation. Across nine representative scoring functions, HiFiPL-Bench revealed reduced performance in scoring, ranking, and most docking evaluations relative to CASF-2016, whereas a controlled screening-like task using computationally generated property-matched decoys produced model-specific gains and losses that altered relative rankings rather than uniformly lowering performance. Model-specific overlap and deoverlap analyses further showed that documented development-data exposure differed substantially among methods and that deoverlapped sensitivity analyses affected models and evaluation tasks nonuniformly. Together, these findings indicate that performance estimates remain sensitive to starting-structure curation, task-specific preparation, data set composition, decoy design, benchmark protocol, and recoverable development-data exposure. HiFiPL-Bench therefore provides a reusable diagnostic framework for evaluating scoring-function performance in a structurally curated and bias-aware benchmark setting.

item.title: FlowBack-Adjoint : Physics-Aware and Energy-Guided Conditional Flow-Matching for Protein Backmapping
item.description:
Abstract
Coarse-grained (CG) molecular models of proteins can substantially increase the time and length scales accessible to molecular dynamics simulations of proteins, but recovery of accurate all-atom (AA) ensembles from CG simulation trajectories can be essential for exposing molecular mechanisms and for the calculation of physical properties requiring atomistic detail. The recently reported deep generative model FlowBack restores AA detail to protein Cα traces using a flow-matching architecture and demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in backmapping of AA structural ensembles (J. Chem. Inf. Model. 65, 2, 672–692, 2025). Training, however, is performed exclusively on structural data, and in the absence of any awareness of interatomic energies or forces, small structural imperfections can produce high-energy backmapped structures. In this work, we introduce FlowBack-Adjoint as a lightweight enhancement that upgrades the pretrained FlowBack model through a one-time, physics-aware post-training pass. Auxiliary contributions to the flow introduce physical awareness of bond lengths, bond angles, and Lennard-Jones interactions, and gradients of a molecular mechanics force field energy are incorporated via adjoint matching to steer FlowBack-Adjoint toward low-energy configurations without compromising structural fidelity or diversity. In benchmark tests against FlowBack, FlowBack-Adjoint lowers single-point energies by a median of ∼30 kcal/mol·residue, reduces errors in bond lengths by >95%, eliminates >97% of molecular clashes, maintains excellent diversity of the AA configurational ensemble, and produces configurations capable of initializing stable all-atom molecular dynamics simulations. In applications to large protein–protein interfaces, including peptide–major histocompatibility complexes (peptide–MHCs) and HIV capsid assemblies, the model improves agreement with molecular dynamics-derived contact frequencies and increases the recall of experimentally observed interactions. We propose FlowBack-Adjoint as an accurate and efficient physics-aware deep generative model for AA backmapping from Cα traces generated by structure prediction tools, coarse-grained simulations, or low-resolution experimental data.

item.title: Benchmark-Optimized Pipeline Identifies Experimentally Validated Antifreeze Peptides in Antarctic Krill
item.description:
Abstract
Antifreeze proteins (AFPs) offer promising prospects as biocryoprotectants, yet their discovery remains a great challenge due to the lack of efficient large-scale screening tools. Here, we present a benchmark-optimized, multimodel computational pipeline that integrates property evaluation and structural assessment for high-throughput AFP identification. Through systematic benchmarking on independent testing data set, two optimal strategies were identified: the two-model-based Strategy 8 achieved the highest accuracy of 0.82, while the stricter four-model-based Strategy 18 attained the highest precision of 0.97, making it optimal for initial large-scale screening. Furthermore, this pipeline was applied to screen 153,359 Antarctic krill sequences and discovered 13 novel antifreeze peptides. Dynamic ice shaping assays revealed that four out of 13 peptides significantly inhibited ice crystal growth. Notably, Peptide 10 (SPHSWANTYQQCK) could inhibit ice growth and recrystallization. This study establishes a robust framework for large-scale AFP identification and provides a set of experimentally validated Antarctic krill peptides with strong potential as novel biobased cryoprotectants.

item.title: An Integrated Coarse-Grained Simulation and Graph-Transformer Framework for the Discovery of Self-Assembling Cyclic Peptides
item.description:
Abstract
Self-assembling cyclic peptides are promising building blocks for functional biomaterials owing to their enhanced structural stability, proteolytic resistance, and diverse supramolecular architectures. However, how cyclization regulates peptide self-assembly remains poorly understood, and computational frameworks specifically developed for cyclic peptides are still lacking. Here, we demonstrate that disulfide-mediated cyclization fundamentally reshapes peptide self-assembly by significantly enhancing aggregation propensity (AP) and promoting the formation of diverse nanostructures compared with their linear counterparts, as confirmed by coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) simulations and experimental characterization. Motivated by these findings, we established an integrated computational-experimental framework for the prediction and rational design of self-assembling disulfide-cyclized peptides. A data set comprising 8,000 cyclic pentapeptides was generated using CGMD simulations, and multiple machine learning and deep learning models were systematically evaluated, among which a Graph-Transformer achieved the best predictive performance (R2 = 0.971). The optimized model was subsequently applied to high-throughput screening of 160,000 cyclic hexapeptides using a ranking strategy integrating AP and hydrophobicity, leading to the identification of multiple previously unreported self-assembling candidates. Experimental validation showed excellent agreement with model predictions. Furthermore, systematic sequence analysis revealed residue- and position-dependent assembly rules unique to disulfide-cyclized peptide systems. This work establishes a computational framework for the rapid discovery of self-assembling disulfide-cyclized peptides and provides new mechanistic insights and design principles for peptide-based functional materials.

item.title: Co-Folding Models Localize Enzyme Active Sites but Fail to Accurately Predict Enzyme–Substrate Complex Structures
item.description:
Abstract
The accurate prediction of enzyme–substrate complex structures is challenging due to the transient and dynamic nature of these interactions. We evaluated the performance of eight machine–learning (ML) docking tools and the physics–based method AutoDock Vina as a reference in the prediction of enzyme–substrate complex structures using a curated data set of 210 diverse, non–redundant enzyme–substrate complexes, equally divided into three classes: metal–free enzymes (A), and enzymes with metal ions outside (B) or inside (C) the active site. All ML–based docking tools had low geometric accuracy and physical plausibility, with fewer than 10% hit rates at the stricter 2 Å threshold for substrate root-mean-square deviation. While no ML-based tools were able to outperform Vina in modeling physically plausible complexes, co–folding tools such as AlphaFold3 and Boltz–2 excelled at active–site localization, and many algorithms performed better for class C enzymes, and worse for class B enzymes. Surprisingly, DynamicBind, which was trained on less data with fewer parameters compared to other models, matched co-folding methods in active-site elucidation. Our results show that enzyme–substrate docking can be affected by the presence of a metal ion, and suggest that better performances for complex structure prediction may be achieved with data-centric strategies including molecular dynamics simulations rather than parameter-heavy ML architectures.

item.title: Martini 3 Coarse-Grained Models for Steroid Hormones
item.description:
Abstract
Steroid hormones are central to the development, metabolism, homeostasis, and reproduction of animals and have been the subject of many evolutionary, ecotoxicological, and human health studies. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CG MD) simulations are a powerful tool to study the structural and dynamic behavior of steroid hormones and their interactions. Here, we expand the capabilities of the widely used Martini 3 CG framework by parameterizing and validating a set of 20 steroid hormone models─including both endogenous and synthetic molecules─to enable their study across diverse targets, systems, and fields of interest. Hormone parameterization followed Martini 3 guidelines, while leveraging the similarities with the parent cholesterol molecule, for which a Martini 3 model is available. Notably, we were able to base our parameterization on the hundreds of experimental structures in the protein data bank that contain steroid hormones, instead of relying on atomistic simulations as is typical with Martini. The parameterized models match to within 5% of target molecular volumes and recover the overall hydrophobicity trend of the hormones, although higher hydrophobicities tended to be overestimated. In free simulations of protein-hormone systems, the experimentally known binding poses could be recovered for 89% of the cases, indicating a successful parameterization also from a functional standpoint. Since several Martini 3 protein models were tested, we also incidentally show that the flexibility of the OLIVES and Go̅Martini models makes them best suited for this type of protein–ligand recognition. Finally, models were validated in interaction with membranes by comparison to reference atomistic data. We expect that the availability of our fully validated Martini 3 CG steroid hormone models will contribute to new studies, collaborations, and applications across different scientific fields.

item.title: Classical Structural Priors Improve Neural Molecular Representations in Molecule Language Models
item.description:
Abstract
Classical molecular similarity is central to chemical information systems, yet molecule-language models trained on paired structure–text data do not necessarily organize molecular embeddings according to graded structural relationships. Here, we introduce Structure-Aware Guided Alignment (SAGA), a training-only regularizer that uses Centered Kernel Alignment to align neural molecular representations with fingerprint-based Tanimoto similarity and requires no additional parameters or fingerprints at inference. In MolCA and Atomas, SAGA improves molecule–text retrieval, retrieves closer structural analogues, and raises average performance in scaffold-split property prediction, without clear degradation of molecular description or text-to-molecule generation. These results, together with control experiments that attribute the gains to the chemical content of the prior, show that established chemoinformatics priors can make molecule-language representations more chemically faithful while retaining their multimodal utility.

item.title: From Molecular Structure to Human Pharmacokinetics: Clearance Prediction Drives Exposure Error in a Hybrid ML–PBPK Workflow
item.description:
Abstract
End-to-end structure-to-exposure workflows combine molecular representation, pharmacokinetic (PK) input prediction, and physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulation, but aggregate accuracy does not reveal where error enters the workflow. We developed graph-based models for predicting plasma unbound fraction, systemic clearance, and steady-state volume of distribution and used paired input substitution in fixed compound-specific PBPK models to trace the downstream effects of these predictions. On held-out benchmark sets, models combining graph-derived and physicochemical features performed comparably to descriptor-based controls, with no detectable paired differences. In 41 compounds, replacing observed clearance with predicted intrinsic or systemic clearance caused the largest deterioration in exposure prediction. AUC0–t 2-fold coverage decreased from 82.9% to between 41.5 and 53.7%, whereas substitutions of physicochemical properties, plasma unbound fraction, and volume of distribution had smaller effects. The intrinsic-clearance and systemic-clearance workflows were not detectably different under matched input slots. Persistent Cmax underprediction with observed inputs indicated an additional limitation in distribution-model structure. When all three PK inputs were predicted, AUC0–t and Cmax were within 2-fold for 41 and 59% of compounds. Because encoder exposure may favor performance in this set, these coverage estimates are upper bounds for unseen chemistry. The paired-substitution design therefore identifies limited clearance prediction accuracy, rather than the PBPK clearance parametrization strategy, as the principal source of exposure error in the evaluated workflow and separates it from residual PBPK structural error.

item.title: Non-B DNA Finder: A Unified Computational Framework for High-Throughput Detection and Contextual Analysis of Noncanonical DNA Structures in Diverse Genomes
item.description:
Abstract
Noncanonical DNA secondary structures arise from unique sequence patterns, and their formation in vivo is modulated by local genomic context, including DNA supercoiling, chromatin state, and transcriptional activity. They contribute fundamentally to DNA replication, transcription dynamics, genome organization, gene regulation, genetic diversity, genome instability, disease pathogenesis, and aging. However, current computational tools for non-B DNA detection are limited in scope. Most predict only one or a few structural classes. None of the tools annotate the novel, structurally distinct and biologically significant motifs characterized in recent years, viz., A-philic DNA, extended-guanine Z-DNA (eGZ-DNA), adenine-cytosine motifs (AC-motifs), and G-triplex intermediates. Furthermore, no existing tool identifies genomic regions where multiple non-B DNA conformations overlap as hybrid domains or coclusters as structural hotspots. In this study we present the Non-B DNA Finder, a high-throughput computational framework that addresses these limitations. It is the first unified platform to integrate the detection of 11 structural classes and 24 subclasses of non-B DNA motifs, encompassing both the classical non-B DNA repertoire and novel motif types. For the first time, it enables genome-wide annotation of hybrid overlap regions and non-B DNA structural clusters. To this end, we applied the pipeline to 11 complete genomes spanning a broad GC range of 17.6–76.2%. A total of ∼15 million non-B DNA motifs were identified, corresponding to an average density of ∼6 motifs/kb (range: 0.76–15.5 motifs/kb). Overall motif density was positively correlated with GC content (r = 0.37). G-quadruplexes were the most prevalent structural class in GC-rich actinobacterial genomes, reaching 7604 motifs/Mb in Miltoncostaea marina. Contrastingly, curved DNA dominated AT-rich endosymbionts, accounting for >70% of all structures in Candidatus Carsonella ruddii and Buchnera aphidicola. Importantly, hybrid interaction analysis revealed that genomic regions rarely encode isolated non-B DNA conformations. In the human genome, G-Quadruplex → i-Motif (9.57%), G-Quadruplex → Slipped DNA (9.46%), and G-Quadruplex → R-loop (5.99%) were the most preponderant hybrid pairs. Structural cluster analysis identified loci harboring up to seven co-occurring structural classes within a 300 bp window. Non-B DNA Finder is freely accessible at https://nonbdnafinder.streamlit.app/, and the source code is available at https://github.com/VRYella/NonBDNAFinder/.

item.title: Molecular Insights into the Allosteric Regulation of Pyruvate Kinase in Streptococcus pneumoniae
item.description:
Abstract
Streptococcus pneumoniae is a clinically important fermentative pathogen that relies heavily on glycolysis for energy production. Its rate-limiting enzyme, pyruvate kinase (SpPYK), is allosterically activated by the effector fructose-1,6-bisphosphate that binds ∼40 Å away from the substrate-binding catalytic site; however, the dynamic mechanism driving this long-range communication remains elusive. In this study, we employ molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and network analysis to map the allosteric activation pathway of SpPYK. Our results indicate that effector binding reshapes the dynamical landscape of the protein, increasing the coherence of collective motions coupled to active-site activation and rewiring long-range correlations. Our computational findings were validated by mutagenesis assays, which confirmed the role of key leucine residues within the activation pathway for the catalytic activity of the enzyme. Our findings refine the “Rock and Lock” model of allostery and offer a structural blueprint for leveraging allosteric regulation to develop species-selective antimicrobials.

item.title: Critical Assessments of Computational Hit-finding Experiments Challenge #4: Targeting the Tyrosine Kinase Binding Domain of the E3 Ligase Casitas B-Lineage Lymphoma Proto-Oncogene B, an Immuno-Oncology Target
item.description:
Abstract
The critical assessments of computational hit-finding experiments (CACHE) are prospective benchmarking exercises where small molecule ligands predicted for a nominated protein of interest are procured and tested experimentally. In CACHE #4, 23 participating teams each selected up to 100 compounds designed to bind the E3 ligase CBLB, an immuno-oncology target. The organizers released the first public structure of CBLB in complex with a known ligand at the outset of the challenge to enable the discovery of chemically novel molecules. Out of the 1688 compounds collectively predicted, ten compounds from nine participants showed some sign of activity (primary hits), but only two were convincingly confirmed (validated hits) across multiple biophysical binding assays and in subsequent analogs, and only one of them was chemically novel. The apparent difficulty of finding novel CBLB ligands, previously reflected by the chemical similarity of inhibitors from the patent literature, suggests that potent CBLB hit molecules were either rare in the screened commercial libraries, or that computational methods may have struggled to retrieve presumably present but weak ligands, or that the conformational dynamics of the binding site was not sufficiently accounted for. The successful method was strikingly atypical. Selection from a chemical binding similarity classifier followed by a random forest binding affinity predictor trained on inhibitors from the patent literature was refined using a diffusion-model binding pose predictor. The road to an ML-driven breakthrough in computational hit-finding can take unexpected turns. Which of these turns reveal novel horizons and which are mere distractions will best be investigated and answered collectively. The discovery in CACHE #4 of a novel series of CBLB ligands is not a trivial achievement and may inform medicinal chemistry efforts toward clinical candidates that complement immune checkpoint inhibition to elicit antitumor immune response in cancer patients.

item.title: VorRel-Net: Topology-Driven Multirelational Learning with Voronoi Contact Area for Protein–Ligand Interaction Site Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Accurate identification of protein–ligand binding sites is a core task in computational biology and drug discovery. Existing protein graph construction methods generally define graph edges using only a single topological distance threshold, ignoring the complementary roles of various noncovalent interactions (such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and long-range salt bridges) in stabilizing protein structures and mediating specific ligand recognition. Furthermore, prevailing models suffer from feature degradation and oversmoothing issues during deep-layer stacking, alongside insufficient capacity for adaptive fusion of multimodal features. To address these bottlenecks, we proposed VorRel-Net (Topology-Driven Multirelational Learning with Voronoi Contact Area for Protein–Ligand Interaction Site Prediction), which constructs a hierarchical multirelational graph to jointly model multimodal residue representations and diverse structural interactions. An adaptive feature evolution mechanism is designed to effectively capture high-order structural dependencies and fuse complementary biological information. In addition, a semantic feedback strategy is introduced to refine low-level representations using high-level semantic guidance, thereby alleviating information loss during deep feature propagation. Experimental results verify that VorRel-Net resolves dimensional mismatch and information redundancy stemming from conventional feature fusion strategies. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art predictive accuracy and biological interpretability on the protein–ligand binding site prediction benchmark.

item.title: Beyond Organic Molecules: MetalLipoDB, a Lipophilicity Data Set for Metal Complexes and Machine Learning Benchmarks
item.description:
Abstract
Lipophilicity governs the uptake, distribution, and toxicity of drug candidates, yet the experimental log P data sets used to build predictive models contain almost exclusively organic molecules. Here we present MetalLipoDB, a manually curated data set of 5158 experimental log P and log D values of complexes of 23 metals from 1192 articles, including 556 entries for multinuclear and heterometallic complexes, annotated with the measurement conditions and counterions. The data set quantifies the interstudy reproducibility of these measurements (0.56 log units) and serves as a benchmark for machine learning, with a mean absolute error of 0.72–0.75 for complexes from unseen articles. For articles with at least four measurements, anchoring the predictions to three measured complexes of the series reduced the error on the remaining complexes from 0.73 to 0.51. MetalLipoDB, the code, and an interactive web application (https://biometaldb.streamlit.app/) are openly available to support the design of metal-based drugs.

item.title: Learning from SILCS FragMaps: Combining Physics-Based Energies with Artificial Intelligence for Rapid Drug Permeability Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Prediction of drug passive permeability represents an important component of rational drug design, requiring continued development of methods to address this problem. Artificial intelligence (AI) methods have long been shown to be of utility for prediction of compound permeability, though they are limited by the range of chemical space in the data sets used in the training of the models. To address this, in the present study, the site identification of ligand competitive saturation (SILCS) methodology is used to calculate free energy profiles for compounds across 3 model lipid bilayers: a POPC–cholesterol bilayer, a bilayer model mimicking parallel artificial membrane permeability assay (PAMPA) experiments, and a bilayer modeling the blood–brain barrier. We present a rapid workflow generating around 15,000 such profiles that accounts for the passive permeation of more than 2500 unique ligands for 3 different membranes. The free energy profiles, which account for all accessible protonation states of the compounds, are then used as features in a collection of AI models. As the physics-based free energy profiles are calculated based on the functional group types in the compounds combined with the SILCS FragMaps calculated for the bilayers, their use potentially improves model transferability by overcoming the limitation of the applicability of the AI models to the chemical space included in the training set, assuming the SILCS-based energies are representative of barriers to compound permeabilities. The resulting models are shown to be almost comparable with available passive permeability models reported in the literature while additionally offering energetic information about the contribution of functional groups to the permeation barriers that may be used for rational compound optimization. Limitations in the cell-based training data, including the presence of drug transporters, are discussed.

item.title: Multiscale Drug–Cell Interaction Modeling via Hybrid Graph Architectures and Knowledge-Aware Fusion for Drug Synergy Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Accurate prediction of drug combination synergy remains challenging due to the vast combinatorial space and strong cellular context dependency of drug responses. To address these limitations, we present MILSyn, a multimodal interaction learning framework designed to capture multiscale drug–cell interactions through three integrated components: (1) relational modeling of heterogeneous graph structures using a hybrid RGCN-GATv2 architecture, (2) cross-modal fusion of biochemical features spanning SMILES, substructures, 3D conformations, and multiomic profiles, and (3) knowledge-aware reasoning via LLM-derived semantic embeddings. Evaluated on DrugComb and four benchmark data sets, MILSyn consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models, demonstrating robust generalization in cold-start scenarios and notable performance gains under few-shot fine-tuning for rare tumors. Attention-based analyses provide exploratory summaries of gene-, pathway-, and substructure-level features associated with the model’s predictions, generating hypotheses for further investigation. By combining scalability with interpretability, MILSyn provides a practical framework for prioritizing candidate drug combinations in precision oncology.

item.title: Alchemy: Bounded Enumeration and Interactive Exploration of Small-Molecule Radical Reaction Networks
item.description:
Abstract
Automated construction of chemical reaction networks is limited by the combinatorial growth of possible molecules, intermediates, and formal transformations. We present alchemy, an open-source Python workflow for systematic enumeration and interactive exploration of small-molecule radical reaction networks. Within an explicitly bounded graph space, alchemy generates connected, neutral C/N/H molecular graphs with single, double, or triple bonds and specified radical counts; RDKit sanitization and canonicalization then remove graph-invalid and duplicate records. Formal reaction candidates are constructed without learned reaction templates by combining bond-dissociation records into rearrangement and transfer stoichiometries. Parallel generation, persistent disk-backed storage, and Kuzu graph representation make the resulting formal network searchable. An independent brute-force control recovers exactly the same 416 neutral molecular graphs as alchemy in a three-heavy-atom C/N/H space. In a trimethylamine case study limited to at most five heavy atoms and one unpaired electron per reaction side, the workflow generated 41,735 unique molecular graphs and a seed-0 bounded sample of 60,035 first-generation reaction records. The reaction construction is not complete because high-frequency shared fragments are handled by a documented deterministic sampling cap. An optional PaiNN molecular-energy model is distributed with the software, but its closed-shell QM9 benchmark does not validate the open-shell species considered here, and its output is not used to rank, filter, or interpret the case-study records. Alchemy therefore, provides a reproducible route to bounded reaction-space construction and downstream graph inspection.

item.title: CadreAI: Agentic AI for Semantically Decoupled Protein–Drug Design and Optimization
item.description:
Abstract
De novo drug design must balance global drug properties with local structural determinants of target specificity. However, existing methods often reduce both objectives to local geometric optimization, relying on blind, reward-driven perturbations that can disrupt essential scaffolds and compromise overall drug-likeness. To resolve this destructive optimization trap, we propose CadreAI, a semantically decoupled agentic de novo drug design framework. CadreAI explicitly decomposes the entire drug design process into two independent subtasks: target-oriented semantic planning and plan-conditioned molecular generation. This strict separation mitigates potential task interference, allowing each module to focus exclusively on its dedicated objective without mutual disruption. Crucially, the strategic logic of how to formulate these target-oriented plans is driven by Simulation-Guided Insight Consolidation (SGIC). To eliminate trial-and-error guessing, this persistent memory mechanism translates transient numerical docking feedback into reusable textual heuristics, allowing the agent to continuously learn and logically deduce subsequent structural edits. Evaluated on the CrossDocked2020 and DrugGen benchmarks, molecules generated by CadreAI achieve superior docking performance with suitable drug-likeness and synthetic accessibility. Additional Boltz-2 evaluations provide orthogonal computational validation of predicted structural plausibility and binding affinity. These results demonstrate that semantically decoupled reasoning offers a highly controllable and practical route for in silico therapeutic design.

item.title: Scramblases and Insertases Facilitate Transmembrane Translocation of Amphiphilic Peptides
item.description:
Abstract
Translocation of amphiphilic peptides across a lipid membrane requires getting polar groups through the hydrophobic membrane core and is therefore prohibitively slow in a protein-free bilayer. Here we show that lipid scramblases can dramatically lower this barrier, effectively acting as bidirectional peptide translocases. Using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, we calculated free energy profiles for the translocation of a model amphiphilic peptide across phospholipid membranes, each containing one of six scramblases or insertases. Most of these proteins reduce the free energy barrier by roughly 80%. Peptide translocation and lipid scrambling share the same mechanism: both proceed along the same hydrophilic groove on the protein surface, and the transition of both is enabled by local membrane defects induced by the groove. We further show that peptide and lipid transport are competitive, and that peptides can inhibit or completely block phospholipid scrambling. Scramblases and insertases thus provide a general route for moving amphiphiles across membranes, and offer a molecular rationale for the cytosolic entry of cell-penetrating peptides.

item.title: Inverse Design of Potential Dicyanamide Anion Based Ionic Liquids with High Nernst–Einstein Conductivity
item.description:
Abstract
Ionic liquids exhibit wide electrochemical windows, negligible volatility, and strong design flexibility, making them promising electrolytes for next-generation energy storage devices. However, the vast design space renders conventional trial-and-error discovery inefficient. Here, we develop a reinforcement learning framework for the de novo inverse design of potential dicyanamide-anion-based ionic liquids with enhanced Nernst–Einstein conductivity. A recurrent neural network trained on known cation structures was coupled with Monte Carlo tree search to generate novel cations. A forward predictive machine learning model was implemented as the reward function, guiding the search toward candidates with high Nernst–Einstein conductivity. Generated structures were subsequently evaluated using molecular dynamics simulations, and the resulting Nernst–Einstein conductivity data were iteratively incorporated to retrain and refine the forward model, forming a closed reinforcement learning loop. Through five iterations, the maximum molecular-dynamics-simulated Nernst–Einstein conductivity of the generated potential ionic liquids increased from 0.61 S/m to 3.77 S/m. The liquid-state character and the synthesizability of the generated candidates remain to be established. The proposed framework could facilitate the computational screening of ionic liquids with desired properties.

item.title: CPPainter: Painting Cell-Penetrating Peptides for Identification and Generation through Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
Abstract
Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) are promising intracellular delivery vectors, but computational CPP identification, sequence optimization, and candidate generation are often studied as separate tasks. This study aimed to develop an integrated framework for CPP prediction and reward-guided sequence design. We developed CPPainter, a computational framework that couples a protein language model ensemble classifier with a reinforcement-learning-guided generator. CPPainter-Classifier outputs a continuous CPP probability score for CPP identification and sequence-level reward assignment. The CPPainter-Generator selects mutation sites with a trainable policy network, proposes amino acid substitutions using a masked language model, and updates the policy through REINFORCE. CPPainter-Classifier achieved a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.9482 on the internal CPPainter-Bench and scores of 0.9002, 0.9348, and 0.7339 on the external CPPCGM-Bench, SiameseCPP-Bench, and MLCPP2-Bench, respectively, outperforming previously reported methods by 1.2 to 7.0 percentage points. Starting from three seed pools, including known CPPs, bacterial signal peptides, and random sequences, the CPPainter-Generator produced 924 high-confidence, strictly novel CPP candidates. The generated candidates successfully reproduced canonical CPP amino acid patterns and physicochemical profiles, achieving Pearson correlations against the positive reference of 0.97 for molecular weight, 0.86 for the Eisenberg hydrophobic moment, and 0.80 for GRAVY hydropathy. CPPainter provides a unified computational framework for CPP identification, sequence optimization, and candidate generation. The generated sequences should be regarded as computationally prioritized CPP candidates and require further experimental validation.

item.title: Ceci n ’ est pas le benzène : The Treachery of Chemical Representations in Machine Learning for Drug Discovery
item.description:
Abstract
Chemists do not draw molecules; they draw agreements about molecules. A hexagon with three alternating lines is not benzene, and, read literally, it is not even an adequate model, since it localizes bonds that experiment treats as equivalent. Chemists repair this discrepancy automatically and never write the repair down; a machine receives the convention, plus whatever further theory its software compiles into it. This Perspective asks what our models actually see, across structural formulas, SMILES, fingerprints, graphs, conformers, simulated ensembles and the token sequences on which chemical language models are trained. We argue that both members of the training pair are representations─one of a chemical entity, the other of an assay-conditioned observation─and interpret tautomeric ambiguity, stereochemical and solid-form identity, activity cliffs, heterogeneous bioactivity labels and generative failure as consequences of this double reduction. We propose accountability, not realism, as the operative standard: explicit entity definitions, complementary representations, assay provenance, calibrated uncertainty, prospective testing. We then make the standard operational, setting out the controlled comparisons that separate representational loss from model limitation, sparse training coverage and experimental heterogeneity, and specifying for each perturbation test the control that makes it interpretable, the criterion for an actionable failure, and the corrective action it implies.

item.title: CROWN: Curated Repository of Well-Resolved Noncovalent Interactions
item.description:
Abstract
The usefulness of structural data sets for machine-learning models of protein–ligand recognition depends not only on their size, but also on how structural imperfections are handled. Existing resources typically trade structural rigor for scale. Recent data sets such as SPINDR improve large-scale structural data through systematic preprocessing, but restrictive inclusion criteria still discard much of the chemical and biological complexity represented in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Here, we present Curated Repository Of Well-resolved Noncovalent interactions (CROWN), a machine-learning–ready data set built around a repair-first curation philosophy: structural inconsistencies are corrected whenever this can be done without compromising experimental evidence at the binding interface, while filtering is reserved for cases that cannot be repaired conservatively. Starting directly from deposited PDB structures, CROWN resolves alternate conformers and connectivity errors, reconstructs complete interaction environments, repairs missing or nonstandard regions outside the binding pocket, assigns protonation states at physiological pH and applies constrained energy minimization using flat-bottomed restraints to relieve local strain while preserving experimentally supported geometry. This strategy yields 193,374 protein–ligand complexes spanning 81,606 PDB entries and 18,516 UniProt accessions, representing more than a 5-fold increase in both complex count and protein diversity relative to SPINDR while retaining a uniform structural representation. Rather than organizing the data set around sparsely available binding-affinity measurements, CROWN adopts a geometry-centric design in which the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms at the binding interface provides the primary source of information. On CASF-2016, CROWN-trained knowledge-based potentials achieved the highest scoring and ranking performance among five training resources, while matching PDBbind- and HiQBind-trained models in docking and screening and consistently outperforming SPINDR-trained counterparts. Together with multiaxis similarity annotations and a companion web interface, CROWN provides a scalable resource for scoring-function development, pose prediction, binder generation, ligand-conditioned protein design, and other structure-based machine-learning applications.

item.title: PertiNet: Interaction-Aware Multimodal Modeling of Protein–Protein Interactions
item.description:
Abstract
Protein–protein interaction (PPI) prediction requires models that combine sequence, structure and functional evidence for proteins excluded from training. We developed PertiNet, which represents these inputs as separate modality tokens, models their interactions and assigns each token a protein-pair-specific weight. On the fixed protein-disjoint Bernett benchmark, PertiNet using sequence and structure achieved AUROC, AUPRC, balanced accuracy and MCC values of 0.71, 0.72, 0.66 and 0.33, respectively. Adding Gene Ontology (GO) annotations increased these values to 0.72, 0.73, 0.67 and 0.35, compared with published TUnA values of 0.70, 0.69, 0.65, and 0.30. Within-study Bernett controls showed that complete fusion improved on concat–MLP with identical sequence and structural inputs, using either the original sequence representation or ESM-2. Matched RBP400 ablations examined the contributions of modalities and fusion components, and Dset_186_72_PDB164 provided a complementary evaluation of residue-level interface localization. These results support integrating structural and functional context with sequence representations through interactions among modality tokens.

item.title: FUSED: A Functional Representation for Joint Structural and Elemental Analysis of Protein–Ligand Binding Sites
item.description:
Abstract
Ligand binding site representations are central to the analysis of protein–ligand interactions, with applications in functional characterization, binding-site comparison, and ligand recognition. Many descriptor-based approaches characterize ligand binding sites using a fixed distance threshold from the ligand, despite substantial variability in how such thresholds are defined and the possibility that relevant structural and compositional information changes across spatial scales. We propose Functional Unification of Structural and Elemental Descriptors (FUSED), a multivariate functional representation that jointly models structural and elemental compositional information on ligand binding sites as functions of distance from the ligand.
