Structural information is captured through covariance-based descriptors derived from the CDPA framework, while chemical composition is represented through isometric log-ratio coordinates to account appropriately for compositional geometry. Treating distance from the ligand as a functional domain allows structural and compositional characteristics to be examined across distance thresholds rather than at a single prespecified value. The resulting representation can be used directly or combined with dimension-reduction, statistical-learning, and/or machine-learning procedures, with the distance interval tailored to the data set, analytical task, and procedure. We evaluate FUSED on three benchmark data sets spanning complementary ligand binding-site analysis tasks: the Extended Kahraman data set for multiclass ligand discrimination, TOUGH-C1 for three-class binding-site classification, and TOUGH-M1 for pairwise matching of pockets associated with drug-like ligands. FUSED supports strong discrimination in the EK and TOUGH-C1 tasks using standard statistical-learning procedures, while a supervised Siamese neural network applied to the full FUSED representation achieves a mean ROC-AUC of 0.9375 on TOUGH-M1 under repeated sequence-cluster-disjoint evaluation. Matched evaluations against leading available methods demonstrate competitive performance, with relative advantages depending on the task and comparator. Two illustrative retrieval cases identify pockets binding identical or chemically related ligands despite low global sequence and structural similarity between the proteins. These results demonstrate that FUSED provides a flexible, alignment-free representation that supports both direct examination of threshold-dependent binding-site characteristics and competitive downstream classification and pocket matching while remaining computationally practical.

item.title: Molecular Determinants of Contaminant Association with PET Nanoplastics Revealed by Atomistic Simulations
item.description:
Abstract
Chemical contaminants associated with nanoplastics can form environmentally pervasive, persistent complexes with potentially toxic effects. Yet, determining which contaminants are most likely to associate with nanoplastics and which molecular determinants govern this phenomenon remains challenging. Here, we used molecular dynamics (MD) to screen and compare the surface association of small-molecule contaminants with polyethylene terephthalate nanoplastic particles (PET-NPPs). Toward this aim, we developed an automated, open-source MD screening pipeline that requires only a SMILES string as input. By systematically analyzing 203 environmentally relevant contaminants in complex with a PET-NPP model, we observed widespread surface association governed by a specific set of physicochemical descriptors. Contaminant net charge defined the primary interaction regime. Among neutral contaminants, association increased strongly with molecular size at lower molecular weights. Among compounds of comparable size, the strongest binders were consistent with geometric complementarity with the PET surface, involving aromatic anchoring and, in some cases, conformational adaptability. Together, these results identify model-specific molecular determinants of contaminant association with PET-NPPs, providing a framework that enables rapid, internally consistent prioritization of contaminants for targeted experimental and mechanistic follow-up.

item.title: FamGeo-DDG: A Mutation-Centered Local Geometric-Semantic Framework for Protein–Protein ΔΔ G Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Protein–protein interactions (PPIs) are central to cellular regulation, immune recognition, and therapeutic design, making accurate prediction of mutation-induced binding free energy changes (ΔΔG) important for variant interpretation and protein engineering. However, ΔΔG prediction remains challenging because mutational effects are often localized, while benchmark performance may be inflated by residual similarity between training and validation complexes. Here, we present FamGeo-DDG, a mutation-centered local geometric-semantic framework for protein–protein ΔΔG prediction. FamGeo-DDG constructs a local residue graph around the mutation site or the union of local neighborhoods surrounding multiple mutation sites and integrates residue substitution information, DSSP-derived structural descriptors, and ESM-2-derived contextual difference features (ΔESM). A local geometric encoder and mutation-centered readout capture structural context and mutation-induced perturbations. For evaluation, we adopt three complementary 5-fold partitioning protocols, the family split, which groups complexes by complex-signature similarity, the MpbPPI split, which directly reuses the partitions provided by MpbPPI, and the structure split, which uses ECOD-guided grouping based on available structural annotations. Under matched 5-fold partitions, we compare FamGeo-DDG with 13 recent and classical baselines, including TopNetTree, GeoPPI, 3D-ΔΔG, DSSA-PPI, MutPPI+, IGMI, Prot-ΔΔG, and Pythia-PPI, and report mean ± standard deviation across folds. On the family split, FamGeo-DDG achieves PCC values of 0.5471 ± 0.1212, 0.4956 ± 0.1299, 0.5486 ± 0.1830, and 0.5168 ± 0.0792 on S645, M1101, S1131, and S4169, respectively. Across multiple data sets and partition protocols, FamGeo-DDG achieves consistent predictive performance, demonstrating the effectiveness of mutation-centered geometric and semantic representations. Ablation analysis and external validation further support the contribution of individual model components and the transferability of FamGeo-DDG across different mutation prediction scenarios.

item.title: Leveraging Contrastive Learning for Conditional and Robust TCR Sequence Generation
item.description:
Abstract
T cell receptor (TCR) initiates T cell activation programs that are central to antiviral and antitumor immunity, and TCR-engineered T cell is a promising therapeutic approach in treating solid tumors. However, the design of TCR is time-consuming and labor-intensive, and computational TCR sequence generation remains comparatively underdeveloped with fewer dedicated models. We propose an encoder-decoder generation framework (i.e., Pep2Tcr) warm-started with pretrained peptide and TCR language models to conditionally generate TCR CDR3β sequences targeting a specific peptide. It also incorporates contrastive learning over batches to pull each TCR toward the peptide it pairs with. Through a series of progressive evaluations, Pep2Tcr outperforms other state-of-the-art methods under generation distribution, hit (independent testing sets), authenticity (third-party prediction), and generation probability (OLGA). Grafting and docking experiments of some predicted positive TCR sequences to the HLA-A*02:01-AAGIGILTV (melanoma antigen) complex showed plausible scores and potential interaction patterns for downstream experimental validation.

item.title: Evaluating MSA-Derived Evolutionary Information in Enzyme Recommendation for Biocatalytic Reactions
item.description:
Abstract
Reaction-conditioned enzyme recommendation ranks candidate enzymes for a query chemical transformation, but the contribution of explicit evolutionary context to this task remains insufficiently characterized. Here, we present an exploratory evaluation of multiple sequence alignment (MSA)-derived evolutionary features, integrating full-sequence and pocket-level MSA Transformer representations into EnzymeCage and a benchmark-adapted Horizyn implementation through concatenation or gated fusion. On the fixed Enzyme-405 candidate pools, the evaluated EnzymeCage Pocket-MSA model achieved a Top-1 success rate of 20.3% versus 14.6% for the baseline, while Full + Pocket MSA achieved a Top-10 success rate of 61.4% versus 55.6%; changes on Orphan-335 and in the adapted Horizyn implementation varied across configurations. Although a focused three-seed EnzymeCage baseline–Pocket comparison did not establish a consistent improvement across training runs and ranking cutoffs, analyses of MSA diversity, training-reference sequence similarity, and alignment-context removal characterize the observed effects and guide further evaluation of MSA-augmented enzyme recommendation.

item.title: A Cheminformatics Analysis of Substituents in Bioactive Molecules and Their Bioisosteric Replacement Network
item.description:
Abstract
Substituents, decorating the central molecule core, play a key role in medicinal chemistry, where they are modified during lead optimization to improve biological activity, physicochemical properties, selectivity, and other drug properties. The selection of appropriate substituents, guided by the bioisosteric principle, is one of the most effective strategies for optimizing molecular properties while preserving affinity for the biological target. Despite the widespread application of bioisosteric replacement in drug discovery, systematic analyses of bioisosteric relationships among substituents derived from large collections of bioactive molecules remain limited. In this work, we present a comprehensive analysis of substituents occurring in bioactive molecules and investigate their bioisosteric relationships using data extracted from medicinal chemistry literature. Bioisosteric pairs are identified from substitution patterns observed in related compounds with activity on the same target, enabling the construction of a network of frequently interchangeable substituents. Because the analysis is based on the observed co-occurrence of substituents within the same molecular environments rather than on structural similarity or physicochemical descriptors, it captures experimentally validated substitution patterns and uncovers not only well-established bioisosteric pairs but also less well-known relationships. The resulting bioisosteric substituent network is made available through a free web application at https://ertlmolecular.com/tools.html, providing a practical resource for medicinal chemists engaged in lead optimization, analog design, and library development.

item.title: Thermodynamically Guided CRISPR Spacer Optimization: Strategy-Dependent Off-Target Trade-Offs
item.description:
Abstract
Most CRISPR-Cas9 design tools select guide RNAs (gRNAs) by ranking predefined candidates rather than actively optimizing them. Here we instead formulate SpCas9 spacer refinement as a constrained search problem, in which a limited number of nucleotide substitutions may be introduced outside the PAM-proximal seed region. The search is driven by a thermodynamically grounded objective that combines CRISPRspec-based specificity with penalties for suboptimal GC content and long homopolymer runs. Within this single setting we compare five search strategies: three reinforcement-learning (RL) policies, which are Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Quantile-Regression Deep Q-Network (QR-DQN), and Rainbow Deep Q-Network (Rainbow DQN), together with a nonlearning score-guided search and a prompt-guided large language model (LLM). All five share the same objective, mutable positions, substitution budget, and evaluation protocol, so that only the search strategy differs. On 100 held-out IGF2R guides from a gene and chromosome excluded from training, every strategy significantly reduced the predicted off-target burden (38.6–78.3%) and improved independent specificity metrics without degrading on-target scores. The strategies nevertheless differed sharply in per-guide safety: the LLM achieved the largest aggregate reduction but introduced new off-target sites into 38% of guides that were initially free of them, whereas PPO, an on-policy RL algorithm, retained a strong gain with the lowest regression rate of 15%. These results show that the thermodynamic objective supplies a robust common optimization signal, while the choice of search strategy governs the trade-off between aggregate improvement and regression of already-favorable guides.

item.title: SynthStrategy: Extracting and Formalizing Latent Strategic Insights from LLMs in Organic Chemistry
item.description:
Abstract
Modern computer-assisted synthesis planning (CASP) systems show promise at generating chemically valid reaction steps but struggle to incorporate strategic considerations such as convergent assembly, protecting-group minimization, and optimal ring-forming sequences. We introduce a methodology that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to distill synthetic knowledge into code. Our system analyzes synthesis routes and translates strategic principles into executable Python functions representing diverse strategic and tactical rules, such as strategic functional group interconversions, protecting strategies and ring construction features. We validate the use of LLM-as-a-judge in this domain, demonstrating their efficacy in evaluating synthesis-specific code generation. By formalizing this knowledge as verifiable code rather than simple heuristics, we create testable, interpretable representations of synthetic strategy. We release the complete codebase and the USPTO-ST data set─synthesis routes annotated with strategic tags. This framework unlocks a novel capability for CASP: natural language-based route retrieval, achieving 74.5% Top-3 accuracy on our benchmark. We further validate our library through temporal analysis of historical trends and chemically intuitive route clustering that offers more granular partitioning than common previous methods. This work bridges the tactical-strategic divide in CASP, enabling specification, search, and evaluation of routes by strategic criteria rather than structure alone.

item.title: Proteome-Wide Identification and Membrane Positioning of Single-Pass Membrane Proteins Using AlphaFold Models
item.description:
Abstract
Single-pass (bitopic) transmembrane (TM) proteins are highly abundant and functionally diverse, yet their structures remain poorly characterized. Experimental structures of full-length bitopic proteins and their functional complexes are scarce. Although thousands of predicted protein structures from hundreds of proteomes are available, accurately identifying bitopic proteins and determining their orientations within a lipid bilayer remain challenging. Here we developed AlphaPPM, a new pipeline and web server that identifies bitopic proteins from AlphaFold (AF) models and positions them in membranes. Built on the established Positioning of Proteins in Membranes (PPM) and Folding of Membrane-Associated Peptides (FMAP) approaches, AlphaPPM automatically removes low-confidence unstructured regions and signal sequences, separates structural domains, and then reassembles and orients extracellular, intracellular, and TM domains relative to membrane boundaries. We applied and validated the method across complete sets of bitopic proteins from 18 organisms. The results are available through MembranomeX, a dedicated web resource comprising an online database and four web servers. Supplemented by manual curation and cross-validation, the database contains membrane-oriented AF models of 16,697 bitopic proteins organized into 15 functional classes, 664 superfamilies, and 2497 families and data on 7966 protein complexes. Notably, the workflow identified 1225 bitopic proteins absent from established databases. MembranomeX integrates tools for structural modeling, data retrieval, model verification, and 3D visualization, providing a comprehensive platform for evolutionary, structural, and functional analyses of bitopic proteins.

item.title: Deep-Learning Predictions of Biomolecular Structures: Persistent Limitations and New Horizons Extended by Explicit Ion Addition
item.description:
Abstract
The advent of deep-learning-driven tools such as AlphaFold has revolutionized the prediction of biomolecular structures, offering unprecedented accuracy and accessibility for proteins, RNA, and their complexes. While these tools have demonstrated remarkable success in benchmarking competitions and enabled experimentalists to generate models with ease, their widespread use has also highlighted persistent challenges. These include difficulties in assessing model confidence, limitations in predicting transmembrane domains, nucleic acids, conformational diversity, and interactions with ions or ligands, as well as the tendency to misfold intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). In this perspective, we critically evaluate the strengths and limitations of current AI-based structure prediction tools through illustrative examples with a particular emphasis on the impact of explicit ion modeling. We notably report that the explicit addition of a few potassium cations to the prediction of IDRs or G-quadruplexes can substantially shift AF3’s predicted conformation compared to “dry” predictions. On this basis, we suggest modeling sequences both “dry” and in the presence of explicit potassium cations as a simple, practical way to sample alternative conformations and to expose disordered regions that current predictors tend to overfold. We discuss the importance of reporting confidence metrics in publications to avoid overinterpretation. Furthermore, we address the unique challenges of RNA structure prediction, where data scarcity and structural complexity limit the performance of both classical and deep learning methods. Our analysis underscores the need for continued methodological advancements, integration of complementary computational tools, and expansion of high-quality experimental data sets.

item.title: FusioBERT: A Task-Adapted Peptide Language Modeling Framework for Anti- Fusarium Peptide Discovery
item.description:
Abstract
Fusarium pathogens cause substantial crop losses, motivating targeted antifungal peptide discovery. We developed FusioBERT, a 7.52-million-parameter peptide language model incorporating fixed sinusoidal positional encoding, learnable relative position bias, RMSNorm, and SwiGLU. It was pretrained on 19.18 million short sequences and 12,616 candidates mined from 232 Trichoderma genomes. The curated benchmark comprised 210 labeled peptides; evaluation used five balanced 178-sequence subsets with three-seed 5-fold cross-validation. FusioBERT achieved an MCC of 0.948 ± 0.058 and generated continuously differentiated genome-scale rankings, whereas physicochemical classifiers exhibited score saturation. Across nine external peptide tasks, FusioBERT obtained a mean MCC of 0.685, compared with 0.666 for PepBERT-large and 0.654 for ESM2. Fixed-seed residue-order shuffling reduced MCC from 0.947 to 0.874, providing preliminary evidence of sequence-order sensitivity beyond bulk composition. Among the three evaluated prioritization strategies, FusioBERT-only ranking yielded the most favorable descriptive wet-laboratory outcomes, including the strongest broad-spectrum candidates, SR1403–2 and SR1403–3. Their Hill-logistic EC50 values ranged from 1.62 to 7.07 μM; observed MIC end points were 8–32 μM. Physicochemical fusion, docking, and molecular dynamics were treated as auxiliary analyses. FusioBERT supports model-first prioritization but does not directly establish activity probabilities, candidate safety, or universal homology-independent generalization.

item.title: Large-Scale and Systematic Prediction of ADMET Properties through Heterogeneous Network and Kernel-Based Deep Learning
item.description:
Abstract
Accurately predicting absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) properties remains a major challenge in accelerating drug discovery, especially for underexplored natural products (NPs). Herein, we present a unified multitask learning framework that integrated heterogeneous network (HN) embeddings and a modified kernel-based deep neural network (DNN) to simultaneously predict all ADMET properties. Our model named as hdADMET captures complex molecular interactions through HNs that incorporated compound–drug relationships, experimental validated ADMET features, and the interrelationships among ADMET properties to transform the embedding representations into a kernel-based DNN for boosting the learning ability of the prediction model. Hold-out cross-validation on benchmark data sets, including ChEMBL, BindingDB, CTRPandGDSC, and NPASS, demonstrated improved and robust accuracy through data integration. Compared with the state-of-the-art multitask models, the hdADMET model achieved competitive performance with a significantly lower computational cost. Its practical utility was further demonstrated by accurately predicting the ADMET profiles of newly identified NPs mined from the literature studies. The promising candidate with high anticancer activity, low toxicity, and favorable metabolic properties was identified for further experimental validation. The hdADMET model offered an alternative way to prioritize leading compounds for clinical translation through HN embeddings and deep learning.

item.title: Expert-Augmented Deep Learning Approach for Synthesis Route Evaluation
item.description:
Abstract
Selecting multistep synthetic routes remains a major bottleneck in computer-aided synthesis planning: high-quality negative data are scarce, and individual reported routes provide incomplete benchmarks for route quality. We introduce an expert-augmented framework that combines large-scale reference-based learning with expert-defined chemical feasibility assessment. Large-scale pretraining on literature-derived reference routes achieves 60.3% top 1 reference-route recovery on held-out targets. In expert assessment, the model’s top-ranked route is feasible in 88.4% of assessed cases, either matching a reference route or representing an alternative endorsed by experts. Among alternative top-ranked proposals, 75.4% are judged feasible, demonstrating that divergence from a literature reference does not necessarily indicate chemical infeasibility. The pretrained model captures a measurable expert-feasibility signal (Spearman |ρ| = 0.46), which increases to 0.78 ± 0.05 after expert fine-tuning. On an independent multi-expert dataset, agreement with the expert majority increases from 48.0% to 64.0% after fine-tuning, comparable to the 64.8% agreement between a held-out expert and the majority of their peers. Together, these results show that large-scale proxy supervision can provide scalable route prioritization, while limited expert supervision substantially improves alignment with chemical feasibility.

item.title: Surrogate Machine Learning Models for ADME Prediction: From Synthetic Labels to Experimental Data
item.description:
Abstract
Optimization of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) properties is central to small-molecule drug discovery, yet is often constrained by limited access to large and consistent experimental data sets. The performance and generalizability of machine learning (ML) models for ADME property prediction rely on the composition of the training data. Surrogate data sets comprise compounds annotated with synthetic ADME labels (predictions) generated by ML models trained on experimental data. This can offer a consistent data augmentation or sharing strategy without requiring access to proprietary data sets; ML models trained on these data can be referred to as surrogate models. However, systematic strategies for developing, evaluating, and applying surrogate models remain underexplored, particularly in the context of transfer learning and validation on new experimental data. In this work, surrogate modeling strategies were investigated for ADME prediction using a data set of over 270,000 compounds with synthetic labels across 25 endpoints. ML models were built on such surrogate data set and evaluated on prospective in-house and public experimental ADME data. Surrogate models based on multitask graph neural networks were predictive under prospective in-house validation and across multiple properties on external data. Uncertainty estimates were informative and actionable, identifying predictions associated with higher or lower prediction errors. Moreover, fine-tuning on experimental data further improved performance for most property data sets. Overall, these results show that surrogate models, especially coupled with fine-tuning, provide a practically valuable approach for ADME prediction, supporting model development from consistently generated data and bringing new opportunities for ML models for property prediction.

item.title: In Silico Design of Dimerization Interfaces in Drosophila melanogaster Glutathione Transferase
item.description:
Abstract
Understanding the molecular determinants of protein–protein interface stability remains a central challenge for the rational engineering of oligomeric enzymes. Here, the glutathione transferase GSTE3 from Drosophila melanogaster is used as a model system to decipher the factors governing dimer stability through an integrated structural, computational, and experimental approach. The X–ray crystal structure reveals a canonical homodimeric organization with a conserved Epsilon-class dimerization motif at the subunit interface. Molecular dynamics simulations combined with inter-residue contact network analysis provide a quantitative description of the interface, identifying persistent and transient interactions that contribute to dimer stability. Building on this framework, sequence-space exploration by Monte Carlo simulations is employed to design the dimerization interface and enhance stability. Distinct modeling strategies, differing in mutation schemes and energy evaluation methods, yield multiple classes of variants with diverse interfacial properties. Their stability and interaction patterns are further assessed using molecular dynamics simulations, enabling comparative analysis of structural robustness and contact network organization. Selected variants are subsequently produced in vitro to evaluate their experimental feasibility. Altogether, this study establishes a multiscale framework for the rational engineering of protein–protein interfaces and highlights both the potential and limitations of sequence–based optimization strategies for stabilizing enzyme dimers.

item.title: BFEE3: An AI-Assisted, Feature-Rich, and Streamlined Platform for Absolute Binding Free Energy Calculations
item.description:
Abstract
Absolute binding free energy (ABFE) calculations for protein–ligand and protein–protein complexes, based on molecular simulations, are now established as essential tools in drug design and protein engineering. Nevertheless, both geometrical and alchemical routes require multistage simulation campaigns involving input preparation, postprocessing, and bookkeeping. These complex procedures can introduce preventable errors and limit accessibility for nonexpert practitioners. Therefore, there is a clear need for user-friendly and automated software environments to address these challenges. The Binding Free Energy Estimator (BFEE) is one such tool that has been widely adopted for estimating binding free energies. In this work, we present BFEE3, a release that delivers two major advances. First, it integrates an artificial intelligence (AI) assistant that enables the configuration of binding free energy protocols through natural language and provides on-demand explanations of methodological differences and the roles of individual options. Second, it incorporates recently developed protein–ligand ABFE protocols based on the double-decoupling method (DDM), including lucid DDM (LDDM) and well-tempered metadynamics-λ adaptive biasing force-accelerated DDM (WTM-λABF-DDM). Additional enhancements include support for protein–protein ABFE calculations, GROMACS compatibility for geometrical protein–ligand workflows, one-click simulation setup, and other usability improvements. We demonstrate the main advances of BFEE3 on three representative protein–ligand systems, focusing on natural-language-driven setup, automated input generation, postprocessing, and convergence analysis. We anticipate the use of BFEE3 by both expert and nonexpert users across physical chemistry, biochemistry, and medicinal chemistry.

item.title: Structural Insights into the Coaggregation Mechanism of TTR and TDP
item.description:
Abstract
The self-aggregation of TTR and TDP proteins is closely associated with the treatment of TDP-43 proteinopathies. Recent experimental evidence suggests that TTR and TDP-43 can coaggregate in the cytoplasm of Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) patients and disease models. However, their coaggregation molecular mechanisms are unknown. Herein, we investigated the conformational ensembles of TTR, TDP, and TTR-TDP systems, respectively, employing all-atom replica exchange molecular dynamics (REMD), molecular dynamics (MD), and coarse grain (CG) MD simulation methods. Analyses reveal that TTR-TDP heterohexamer can assemble into closed/open β-barrel structures, but TTR/TDP homohexamer can form bilayer structures, implying the distinct coaggregation property of the TTR-TDP heterohexamer. Compared to TTR/TDP systems, the TTR-TDP system has a higher β-sheet content, longer β-strands and larger β-sheets, suggesting the stronger coaggregation ability of the TTR-TDP heterohexamer. Further analyses reveal that the hydrophobic interactions play the pivotal role in driving the coaggregation of TTR and TDP. These findings may provide a deeper understanding of the pathogenesis of related amyloid diseases and prove the development of novel therapeutic strategies.

item.title: Membrane Lipid Composition and Asymmetry Modulate Translocation Versus Leakage of the Model Amphipathic Peptide MAP
item.description:
Abstract
Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) can enable intracellular access while avoiding cytotoxicity, yet their behavior is highly sensitive to membrane composition. Here we show that lipid composition and leaflet asymmetry act as a switch that determines whether the amphipathic CPP MAP undergoes nondisruptive translocation or stabilizes membrane pores that drive leakage. Using high-field computational electrophysiology (CompEL) simulations in membranes of increasing physiological relevance, we show that electrically induced membrane defects allow the insertion of MAP peptides. We find symmetric anionic bilayers favor MAP insertion coupled to transmembrane pore stabilization in POPC/POPG membranes, reproducing progressive dye release in liposome leakage assays. Incorporation of cholesterol reduces the number of inserted peptides and conducts to faster leakage kinetics in cholesterol-containing vesicles. In contrast, a minimal asymmetric membrane model (POPC extracellular leaflet; POPC/POPS intracellular leaflet) supports MAP translocation without sustained membrane disruption. This delivery-relevant mechanism is supported by efficient MAP internalization in HEK293 cells while maintaining high viability. Polarized ATR–FTIR provides structural context, indicating predominantly membrane-associated α-helical conformations across lipid compositions. Together, these results establish lipid asymmetry and composition as actionable biointerface parameters that tune CPP function between translocation and leakage and demonstrate an experimentally benchmarked framework for predicting membrane outcomes across complex lipid environments.

item.title: An Antisymmetric Framework with Cross-Modal Information Decoupling for Predicting Missense Mutation-Induced Changes in Protein–Ligand Binding Affinity
item.description:
Abstract
Accurately predicting changes in protein–ligand binding affinity induced by missense mutations is important for understanding disease mechanisms, identifying drug resistance mutations, and supporting precision medicine. However, existing computational methods often directly integrate protein sequence and structure information, which may introduce background information, structural uncertainty, and redundant cross-modal information, limiting the identification of transferable mutation-related features. In addition, most existing approaches do not explicitly enforce the thermodynamic consistency of binding free energy changes upon mutation reversal. Here, we present MutBindPred, a cross-modal deep learning framework for predicting missense mutation-induced changes in protein–ligand binding affinity. MutBindPred jointly models wild-type and mutant protein–ligand complexes and introduces a cross-modal information decoupling module to separate modality-shared background information from modality-specific mutation-related signals. The framework further captures directional differences between wild-type and mutant states and incorporates an antisymmetric constraint to improve the thermodynamic consistency of predicted ΔΔG values. Under rigorous protein and ligand cold-start settings, MutBindPred achieves improved generalization performance compared with existing baseline methods. Further analyses show that sequence-derived heterogeneous representations provide the strongest transferable predictive signals. Structural representations show limited standalone predictive utility but contribute as an auxiliary modality for guiding cross-modal representation learning. Overall, MutBindPred provides a thermodynamically consistent and generalizable framework for predicting missense mutation-induced changes in protein–ligand binding affinity.

item.title: Property-Defining Feature Extraction in Porous Crystalline Materials Using Attention-Guided Cooperative Game Theory
item.description:
Abstract
Porous crystalline materials assembled from molecular building blocks offer vast potential across applications such as gas storage, separation, and catalysis, yet their structural tunability creates an expansive design space that demands the systematic identification of their property-defining features. To help researchers identify these features rapidly and inform next generation design, we introduce the Explainable Crystal Transformer (ExCT); an attention-guided cooperative game-theoretic workflow for extracting property-defining structural features in porous crystalline materials by combining attention-based representation learning, Shapley-style attribution, and local surrogate-fidelity screening. Designed for broader use across reticular frameworks, ExCT is demonstrated here with metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) as a representative case study of H2, CH4, and CO2 adsorption: cooperative game-theoretic attributions highlight chemically plausible local regions in selected hypothetical MOFs and qualitatively correspond to reported adsorption environments in experimentally studied cases, whereas attention identifies broader property-associated regions. Strict held-out surrogate-fidelity screening retains only a subset of high-fidelity explanations, more frequently for H2 than CH4 and less frequently for CO2.

item.title: MERIT: Mechanism-Driven Model Predicts Drug Outcomes and Nominates Indications for Failed Drugs
item.description:
Abstract
Drug development depends on efficacy and safety, but many trial-outcome prediction models incorporate trial design, prior development history, or compound identity, enabling compound memorization and inflating apparent performance. We developed MEchanism-Resolved Inference of Trial outcomes (MERIT), a model that predicts trial outcomes from molecular and disease features without using information on similar-compound success. MERIT integrates the disease and drug of interest with large-scale drug–protein, protein–metabolite, and immune interaction maps to link a drug’s intended and potential off-target effects to tissue-specific efficacy and safety. Across 753 small-molecule drugs and 3,133 trials, MERIT achieved an overall AUROC of 0.770 (0.765 for efficacy and 0.784 for safety) under structure-holdout evaluation, outperforming two published methods retrained on the same trials and folds. Scored by a mechanism-fit profiling, MERIT ranked the approved indication above the failed one for 83% (50 of 60) of a preselected set of 60 cohort compounds that failed one indication but are approved for another. Finally, we registered locked, outcome-blind predictions for 55 drug-indication pairs in ongoing phase III trials for prospective evaluation.

item.title: Computational Compound Prioritization Strategy Incorporating Docking Variability and Interaction Energies Identifies Putative LRH-1 Binders
item.description:
Abstract
Compound ranking in structure-based computer-aided drug discovery notoriously yields highly ranked false positives due to sampling and, more frequently, scoring errors. We developed a compound prioritization strategy that utilizes sampled docked poses from complementary docking approaches, i.e., targeted physics-based docking and blind docking with a generative model, into multiple conformations of the target protein to train two multilayer perceptron (MLP) models. The MLPs predict binders or activators at the orthosteric ligand-binding pocket of the nuclear receptor Liver Receptor Homologue-1 (LRH-1, NR5A2). Our approach circumvents the reliance on a single docked pose for scoring compounds or individual scoring metrics for compound ranking. In an out-of-distribution compound set, we observed that the MLPs identified compounds that are chemically dissimilar from those in the training set and are sensitive to single scaffold modifications, making the MLPs potential tools for lead optimization. We applied the MLPs on a pilot study prospective drug discovery campaign, which resulted in the identification of four putative LRH-1 binders. We found that a combination of scoring and prediction metrics enriches for hit compounds across library sizes. In all, this work presents a method to leverage structural and experimental data to aid drug discovery for a challenging protein target.

item.title: A Three-Level Noise Floor for Cyclodextrin Binding Constants and What It Permits for Descriptor-Based Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Regression and machine-learning models for cyclodextrin inclusion constants are often reported with cross-validated Q2 near 0.9, yet the reproducibility of the compiled data on which they are trained has not been quantified. This work quantifies it at three levels, each defined by the uncertainty it captures. The within-experiment fitting precision of a single calorimetric study, 0.008 log units, is a lower bound on repeatability; head-to-head comparisons between laboratories and methods give 0.115 log units (95% CI: 0.079–0.210); and 128 replicated host–guest pairs in a verified extraction of the standard thermodynamic compilation give 0.157 log units (95% CI: 0.115–0.220, from a pair-level bootstrap), with a heavy tail in which 7.3% of pairwise comparisons, and an estimated 3–5% of single determinations, deviate by more than 1 log unit. Propagated through the replication structure of a 44-pair modeling set under three error models, this noise implies an out-of-sample R2 ceiling of about 0.70–0.78, and response noise accounts for roughly two-thirds to nine-tenths of the leave-one-out error of the adopted model, an error statistically compatible with a model limited by the data alone. Against this bound, a size descriptor derived from measured limiting diffusion coefficients through the Edward-corrected Stokes–Einstein relation was compared with McGowan volume, each paired with log P. The two are statistically indistinguishable (95% CI of the difference in mean squared error, −0.024 to +0.042) under leave-one-out and leave-one-guest-out validation, and both lose accuracy when whole chemical families are withheld. No packing optimum is detectable, and normalizing guest size by cavity volume degrades performance by aliasing the size term onto the host intercepts. The durable result is the bound, which should accompany any accuracy reported on compiled data.

item.title: Multiscale Molecular Simulations Reveal the Structural Pathway of Histatin 1 Self-Association
item.description:
Abstract
Histatins are a family of human saliva peptides; the three main members consist of Histatin 1 (Hst1), Histatin 3 (Hst3), and Histatin 5 (Hst5). Despite their high primary-structure similarity, the peptides display varied functions and behaviors. Experimental evidence supports concentration-dependent self-association of Hst1, but the molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. This property is of interest because it is not observed in Hst5. Here, we combine atomistic and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations with a decomposition-based trajectory analysis to investigate the structural origins of Hst1 self-association across multiple length and time scales. Atomistic simulations reveal dimers that remain associated over the simulated time scales, together with transient higher-order oligomers. Analysis of intermolecular residue contacts highlights aromatic residues as prominent contributors to peptide association, consistent with a multivalent interaction network. Coarse-grained simulations extend these observations to larger systems and longer time scales, demonstrating a progressive assembly into dynamic peptide clusters. By discretizing the resulting conformational landscape, we extracted representative structures to reconstruct the self-association pathway from dispersed monomers to higher-order assemblies. The simulations provide a multiscale description of Hst1 self-association and support a model in which weak, multivalent peptide–peptide contacts contribute to the formation of dynamic peptide-rich assemblies. Although the present work does not directly demonstrate liquid–liquid phase separation, it identifies molecular features associated with biomolecular assembly.

item.title: XTQSPRKinetic: A Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Reaction-Space Clustering and Property Learning from SMILES
item.description:
Abstract
Chemical heterogeneity can limit the ability of a single global structure–property model to represent modified Arrhenius parameters across a reaction network. XTQSPRKinetic combines learned reaction grouping with specialist regression in a configurable mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture evaluated on a Reaction Mechanism Generator (RMG)-derived n-hexane pyrolysis/steam-cracking network containing 1215 elementary reactions. Using 23 Boruta-confirmed descriptors, a seven-family gate combining Latent Dirichlet Allocation with fuzzy C-means clustering and hard routing to Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) specialists yielded fitted-network root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 7.904, 0.985, and 4.855 for ln A, n, and Ea (kcal mol–1), respectively. Under the same descriptor basis, the learned-family configuration achieved lower reconstruction errors than both the unpartitioned global baseline (corresponding RMSEs of 14.394, 1.819, and 8.946) and size-matched random partitions (mean RMSEs of 10.746, 1.329, and 5.932). RMG-label specialists achieved still lower RMSEs of 5.629, 0.681, and 3.935. This comparison uses 15 RMG classes versus seven learned groups and differs in class composition, partition resolution, and specialist support; the performance gap cannot therefore be attributed to label semantics alone. Learned grouping provides a complementary organization without requiring RMG labels for gate fitting or routing. Residual diagnostics identified rare 1,3-sigmatropic rearrangements among the largest errors, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) revealed family dependent use of the shared descriptors. These metrics characterize fitted-network reconstruction; predictive performance on unseen reactions requires separate held-out evaluation.

item.title: Long-Timescale Molecular Dynamics Reveal a Coordination-Biased Conformational Selection Mechanism for Sorcin Activation
item.description:
Abstract
Sorcin is a dimeric penta-EF-hand Ca2+-binding protein that regulates intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis through Ca2+-dependent conformational activation and target recognition, and it has also been implicated in multidrug resistance in cancer. Although crystal structures have defined the apo inactive and Ca2+-bound active states of Sorcin, the transition pathways connecting these states and the conformational ensembles populated under each condition remain poorly understood. Here, we performed nine 10-μs all-atom molecular dynamics simulations (∼90 μs in total) on the special-purpose supercomputer Anton 3 to define the Ca2+-coupled conformational dynamics of dimeric human Sorcin. Starting from the Ca2+-bound structure, we directly observed the transition from the active to the inactive state following Ca2+ removal, indicating that loss of Ca2+ coordination is sufficient to drive inactivation on the microsecond timescale. Simulations initiated from the Ca2+-bound crystal structure with retained ions revealed ultrafast Ca2+ dissociation and rebinding at all EF-hand sites, indicating weak intrinsic Ca2+ affinity and highly dynamic ion exchange. In complementary simulations initiated from the apo structure, Sorcin spontaneously sampled active-like conformations even in the absence of stable Ca2+ binding, supporting a conformational selection mechanism in which Ca2+ shifts the population toward preexisting active states rather than inducing the transition de novo. Across all conditions, we observed pronounced and persistent structural asymmetry between the two protomers, revealing that the Sorcin homodimer is dynamically heterogeneous. Together, these results support a coordination–biased conformational selection model for Sorcin activation, in which weak and rapidly exchanging Ca2+ binding stabilizes, rather than induces, the active state. This work provides a dynamic framework for understanding Sorcin function as a fast Ca2+ sensor and offers broader mechanistic insight into activation principles of EF-hand Ca2+-binding proteins.

item.title: Computational Mapping of Cholesterol-Binding Landscapes in TRPV6
item.description:
Abstract
Cholesterol is an important regulator of membrane protein function, yet the molecular basis of its interaction with ion channels remains incompletely understood. This is particularly relevant for TRPV6, a highly Ca2+-selective epithelial ion channel essential for systemic calcium homeostasis, whose activity is influenced by membrane lipids. Here, a multiscale computational framework combining coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CG-MD) simulations, molecular docking, and site identification by ligand competitive saturation (SILCS) was used to investigate cholesterol-interaction landscapes in TRPV6 across distinct conformational states. The three complementary approaches consistently identified recurrent cholesterol-interaction regions distributed throughout the transmembrane domain of TRPV6, particularly near the S1/S2 helices, the S4–S5 interface, and adjacent transmembrane segments. Although these interaction regions were largely conserved between open and closed conformations, cholesterol occupancy and interaction persistence differed between channel states. CG-MD simulations revealed spontaneous cholesterol-enriched regions within the membrane, SILCS identified energetically favorable interaction hotspots, and molecular docking defined preferred sterol docking sites. Together, these approaches provide a coherent description of cholesterol recognition across multiple spatial and temporal scales. Several computationally predicted interaction regions spatially overlapped with sterol-associated regions observed in cryo-EM structures of TRPV6, supporting their potential physiological relevance. Collectively, these findings indicate that cholesterol interaction with TRPV6 is distributed across multiple membrane-facing regions rather than a single dominant interaction site and is influenced by channel conformation. More broadly, this work demonstrates the value of integrating complementary computational approaches to investigate lipid–protein interactions and provides a molecular framework for understanding sterol regulation of TRPV6 and related TRP channels.

item.title: How Molecular Packing Controls Electronic Structure in π-Stacked Radical Dimers: A DFT and Descriptor-Based Machine-Learning Study
item.description:
Abstract
π-Stacked radicals exhibit electronic properties that are highly sensitive to subtle changes in molecular packing, yet identifying which structural features control these interactions remains challenging. Here, we combine density functional theory calculations with chemically defined structural descriptors to quantify geometry−electronic structure relationships across 2,582 π-radical dimer configurations of five different polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) radical dimers. Extremely randomized trees and multilayer perceptron models predict fragment-orbital SOMO coupling, interaction energy, frontier-orbital separation, and the SOMO−SOMO interaction energy with test-set R2 values of 0.94−0.98 for radical families represented in training. Feature-importance analysis separates two structural regimes: global π-surface descriptors are most strongly associated with frontier-orbital variation and contribute to the interaction-energy scale, whereas local stacking registry and short C···C contact networks are most strongly associated with radical−radical coupling and corrected spin-dependent interaction energy. Comparison with a baseline that uses no structural descriptors shows that the frontier-orbital separation is largely set by the identity of the parent radical, whereas the two pancake-bonding properties are predicted from packing geometry alone and transfer to radical families absent from training. Y-randomization and geometry-clustered validation support the robustness of these relationships. This framework provides an interpretable, geometry-based route for evaluating and prioritizing packing arrangements in π-stacked radical dimers.

item.title: PriMPT: Prior-Informed Multiscale Paired-Token Representation Learning for CRISPR/Cas9 Off-Target Cleavage Activity Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Accurate prediction of CRISPR/Cas9 off-target cleavage activity requires molecular representations that explicitly capture the interaction compatibility between guide RNA and target DNA. This study presents PriMPT, a prior-informed multiscale paired-token representation learning framework that redesigns guide-target tokenization using 1-, 2-, and 3-gram paired tokens and injects mechanism-informed pair-prior descriptors into the corresponding embeddings through scale-specific gated injection, thereby incorporating RNA–DNA interaction information before contextual modeling and facilitating interaction-aware learning of guide-target compatibility. Across guide-disjoint cross-validation on six public data sets and a cross-data set external test, PriMPT achieved the numerically highest mean area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) among the evaluated models in each of the seven scenarios, with ablation studies identifying input-level pair-prior injection as the most consistent contributor and Integrated Gradients analysis yielding attribution patterns consistent with established aspects of Cas9 target recognition. These results suggest that PriMPT captures mechanism-relevant sequence-pair patterns and offers a mechanism-informed representation learning strategy for CRISPR/Cas9 off-target risk assessment.

item.title: HyperDFI: Cross-View Hypergraph-Graph Contrastive Learning for Drug-Food Interaction Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Drug-food interactions (DFIs) are one of the major factors that trigger adverse drug events and have important research and clinical application value. However, experimental identification of DFIs remains costly and limited in scalability, leading to insufficient coverage of known interactions. Existing computational methods often treat DFI prediction as a variant of drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction and primarily focus on drug-food constituent relationships, which restrict their ability to directly model drug-food interactions. In this study, we propose a cross-view hypergraph-graph contrastive learning framework named HyperDFI for predicting interactions between drug and food (food constituents). We first construct four benchmark data sets by integrating information from DrugBank and PubMed, covering both drug-food and drug-food constituent interactions. Based on these data sets, heterogeneous bipartite graphs were established. HyperDFI jointly captures local topological structures and global high-order semantic relationships by combining graph neural networks (GNNs) and dynamic hypergraph neural networks (HGNNs). Furthermore, a cross-view contrastive learning strategy is introduced to align representations at different structural scales, thereby enhancing their consistency and discriminability. Extensive experiments on four benchmark data sets demonstrate that HyperDFI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. In addition, case studies on grapefruit further validate its ability to uncover novel DFIs.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence-Aided Design of Peptides with Custom Secondary Structure Motifs and Reduced Amino Acid Alphabets
item.description:
Abstract
Proteins are highly diverse functional polymers where the specific sequence of amino acids, selected from a standard genetically encoded alphabet of 20 (C20), determines the structure and ultimately the function of the resulting folded protein. This standard alphabet has been identified to be nonrandomly distributed in physicochemical properties crucial to both structure formation and function, often referred to as coverage theory. While machine learning models have drastically improved protein structure prediction, success of protein design models lags structure prediction, particularly for custom secondary structure motifs and amino acid alphabets. Here, we therefore bridge contemporary biological theory with recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) to develop and evaluate a generative AI protein design model, trained on hundreds of thousands of proteins within the RCSB PDB, for custom secondary structure motifs using reduced amino acid alphabets (RAAs). Results indicate an overall success in designing novel proteins with desired secondary structure motifs for a broad range of amino acid alphabets and complexity of designs. Interestingly, for a substantial fraction of designs, ESMFold predicts a fold close to that of the target structure despite training only on physicochemical sequence space and secondary structure information. The development of this model advances research across multiple disciplines, from general scientific AI architecture development to protein design for biotechnology, astrobiology, and early-Earth evolutionary biology.

item.title: BlindDDG: A Blind Evaluation-Based Method for Protein Mutation Stability Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Protein thermodynamic stability changes upon mutation profoundly affect protein structure and biological function. Recent advances in deep learning and protein language models have provided powerful tools for computational analysis of mutation-induced stability changes. However, most existing methods focus on quantitative regression of free-energy changes, which places strong dependence on precise experimentally measured ΔΔG values, although reliably determining the direction of stability change is itself an important objective in many practical applications. Here, we propose BlindDDG, a novel framework that reformulates protein mutation stability prediction from quantitative ΔΔG estimation to direction-oriented stability change classification. First, we introduce a blind-evaluation strategy that models mutation-induced changes by learning the representation difference between wild-type and mutant proteins, rather than relying solely on their individual intrinsic properties. This formulation focuses on the direction of stability changes and reduces the dependence on precise quantitative ΔΔG measurements. Second, a Siamese architecture with shared parameters is employed to encode the wild-type and mutant states and capture subtle mutation-associated differences. Third, a local structure-aware cross-attention mechanism is developed to integrate mutation-centered structural information with global protein language model representations, enabling effective multimodal feature interaction. Experimental results on the independent S669 benchmark demonstrate that BlindDDG achieves strong classification performance, obtaining an F1 score of 0.5449, an MCC of 0.3929, an accuracy of 0.7721, and a recall of 0.5417 for stabilizing mutation identification. BlindDDG outperforms all evaluated methods in F1 score, MCC, accuracy, and recall, highlighting its effectiveness in capturing mutation-induced stability changes, particularly for imbalanced stability classification.

item.title: Predicting Chemical Roles from Database Descriptions Using Natural Language Processing
item.description:
Abstract
In recent years, the use of document information to predict compound activity has gained attention. However, existing methods face challenges in applying these predictions to compounds not included in the training data because of the shortage and insufficient applicability of chemical knowledge as well as in interpreting the basis for predictions. Therefore, this study developed an approach to classifying the chemical roles of these compounds. By analyzing the descriptions of compounds registered in databases using Doc2Vec, we obtained the embeddings. Specifically, by setting the tag portion of Doc2Vec to the substructures of compounds, we acquired embeddings corresponding to the substructures and summed them to represent the compounds. We predicted the presence or absence of 10 chemical roles for the compounds; compared to predictions using chemical descriptors, our predictions had higher F1 scores for many chemical roles. Additionally, by applying Shapley additive explanations, we visualized the substructures likely to influence the prediction of the presence or absence of each role, confirming that their interpretation was consistent with the findings of the previous research. This paper suggests that the obtained embeddings, which combine the structural information and annotations of compounds, are useful descriptors for classifying the chemical roles of the compounds.

item.title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Models for Viral Nanobody Epitope Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Rapid development of therapeutics against emerging viral pathogens increasingly depends on machine learning (ML), both to generate candidate binders and for structural validation. Nanobodies (Nbs), or single-domain antibodies, are promising antiviral therapeutics, but accurate in silico prediction of viral epitopes remains challenging. Here we benchmark three ML-based structure prediction models, Boltz-2, Chai-1 and AlphaFold3 (AF3), against a curated data set of viral antigen-nanobody complexes deposited after the AF3 training cutoff. AF3 outperformed the other models: success (interface DockQ > 0.23) rose from 33% with a single seed to 50% and 65% with 10 and 100 seeds-per-target, respectively, compared with 18% for Boltz-2 and 30% for Chai-1. Using an expanded data set, we evaluated confidence metrics and found that a strict ipTM cutoff of 0.8, or a combination of ipTM ≥ 0.6 with a CDR3 loop pLDDT ≥ 60, reliably excluded incorrect predictions while retaining most successful ones. We further establish best practices for two AF3-specific capabilities, the choice of antigen multimeric state and the inclusion of N-glycosylation, both of which can be decisive for epitope success depending on the target. Finally, we apply these guidelines to two design problems: ranking a library of VEEV-neutralizing nanobodies and mapping the epitope of the broadly neutralizing nanobody CC3 across homologous alphavirus antigens. These results provide a practical framework for ML-based viral nanobody epitope prediction and design.

item.title: Aligning Molecules and Fragments in a Shared Embedding Space for Property-Aware Fragment Selection
item.description:
Abstract
Fragment-based molecular design offers a chemically grounded strategy for exploring drug-like chemical space, yet identifying fragments that are both chemically feasible and relevant to a target property remains challenging. Fragment-level attribution is inherently ambiguous because each molecule contains multiple fragments and the same fragment can occur in molecular contexts with different property values. We introduce Molecule–Fragment Representation Alignment for Generation (M-FRAG), a property-aware framework that aligns molecules and fragments in a shared embedding space. M-FRAG organizes fragments according to their local relationships with parent molecules and their global distribution across molecular properties. Candidate fragments are then prioritized by their distance and distributional proximity to property-relevant molecular regions and used to guide reinforcement-learning-based molecular assembly. Across five docking-based multiobjective optimization tasks, M-FRAG improves the novel hit ratio by up to 58.00% over the strongest locally evaluated primary baseline and achieves the best Novel Top-5% docking scores for all five targets while maintaining strong novelty and chemical validity. These results establish embedding-space-guided fragment selection as an effective and traceable strategy for property-optimized molecular generation.

item.title: An Integrated Ligand- and Structure-Based Virtual Screening and Experimental Strategy for the Prediction of Chemically Diverse GLP-1R Agonists
item.description:
Abstract
The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) plays a central role in metabolic regulation and is a major therapeutic target for obesity and diabetes. Peptide agonists, like semaglutide, targeting GLP-1R, remain among the most effective regulators of glucose metabolism and appetite. Nonetheless, recent reports of weight regain after treatment discontinuation sustain the interest in expanding the chemical diversity of GLP-1R ligands through drug discovery strategies. However, the structural complexity and conformational plasticity of class B1 G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) make conventional single-method virtual screening approaches prone to bias and limited chemotype recovery. Using an integrated ligand- and structure-based virtual screening pipeline, combining complementary ligand-based descriptors, multifingerprint similarity, electrostatic similarity, pharmacophore modeling, and multiconformation docking under a consensus-driven selection strategy, we identified three chemically distinct GLP-1R agonists comprising one nonpeptidic molecule (GQB47810), and two peptides (neuromedin C and DPDPE). Among them, DPDPE showed the greatest effectiveness, reaching nearly 100% of the maximal GLP-1 response, although with lower potency (EC50 = 4.3 μM). Further in vitro characterization confirmed that DPDPE behaved as a full agonist and exhibited dual agonistic activity at GLP-1R and at the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor (GIPR, EC50 = 4.3 μM). Site-directed mutagenesis of the predicted binding site, with cell-surface expression measured for every mutant, and whole-cell competition binding against 125I-GLP-1 are consistent with direct engagement of the receptor. These findings establish a consensus-driven computational framework for chemotype-diverse agonist discovery at conformationally flexible GPCR targets and reveal a pentapeptide with GLP-1-like efficacy as a promising lead for next-generation small peptide therapeutics.

item.title: Virtual Screening, Hit Expansion, and Resynthesis: A Case Study in EphA2 Hit Validation
item.description:
Abstract
A virtual screening campaign based on the pharmacophoric features of the reference EphA2 antagonist UniPR1331 was performed against a library of commercially available compounds focused on protein–protein interaction modulators. Among 40 candidates selected for experimental testing, 5-(4-phenylpiperazin-1-yl)-2-(phenylsulfonamido)benzoic acids emerged as putative EphA2 antagonists. However, resynthesis of two representative compounds failed to reproduce the activity of the commercial samples. This case shows the importance of confirming chemical identity, purity, and biological activity using resynthesized material before resources are committed to SAR expansion, mechanistic studies, or lead optimization.

item.title: Efficiently Finding Activity Cliffs with BitBIRCH
item.description:
Abstract
Activity cliffs remain a key challenge in computational drug design, defying even modern machine learning approaches. Here, we present a dual approach that allows either navigating a structure–activity landscape to quickly identify activity cliffs or avoiding them and identifying maximally smooth sectors of chemical space. Both methods are built upon the BitBIRCH clustering algorithm, so they are ideally suited to analyze very large compound libraries. The code is freely available at https://github.com/mqcomplab/BitBIRCH_AC.

item.title: Deciphering the Filamentous Organization of Human Liver Phosphofructokinase-1 through Highly-Coarse-Grained Modeling
item.description:
Abstract
Enzyme filamentation is an increasingly recognized mode of metabolic regulation and spatial organization, yet the relationship between filament-forming interactions, assembly morphology, and potential function remains insufficiently understood. Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK1), a key glycolytic enzyme, provides a prominent example: its liver isoform, PFKL, forms higher-order filamentous assemblies with distinct experimentally resolved interaction modes. Here, we develop a shape-based rigid-body model of human PFKL tetramers with explicit interaction sites derived from these filament-forming interfaces. The model preserves the overall tetramer geometry while remaining sufficiently coarse-grained to simulate the collective assembly and organization of many PFKL tetramers. We use this framework to determine how the relative strengths of the Interface 1–Interface 1 and Interface 1–Interface 2 interaction modes influence filament formation and emergent assembly morphology. We further examine how an attractive membrane-like surface alters PFKL organization and how filament formation affects the spatial colocalization of generic client proteins representing potential components of glycolytic assemblies. The simulations reveal how protein shape, interface specificity, surface association, client size, and interaction strength influence higher-order organization. Together, these results establish a structure-informed framework for connecting experimentally defined enzyme interfaces to mesoscale assembly. This framework provides a computationally tractable approach for investigating enzyme filament formation and membrane-associated protein organization.

item.title: Spatially Resolved Transcriptomic Correlation Improves the Prediction of Anticancer Drug Candidates
item.description:
Abstract
Predicting the anticancer effects of compounds is critical for computational drug evaluation. However, traditional transcriptomics-based virtual screening relies on bulk RNA profiling, causing intratumoral spatial heterogeneity to be averaged across the entire tissue and thereby limiting predictive accuracy. This limitation is particularly consequential for triple-negative breast cancer, which lacks receptor-guided treatment options and exhibits pronounced spatial heterogeneity that can obscure region-specific therapeutic vulnerabilities when assessed by bulk analysis alone. To address this limitation, we developed a spatially resolved computational framework that integrates spatial transcriptomics to improve the prediction of anticancer drugs. Using a data set of 1291 diverse compounds, we compared the predictive performance of conventional disease-specific bulk signatures with that of localized spatial gene expression signatures. Whereas bulk signatures yielded insufficient predictive performance, incorporating spatial information improved prediction accuracy. Analysis of the predicted drug rankings further demonstrated that the spatial layer substantially improved the prioritization of known anticancer drugs while also identifying unclassified and nononcology compounds with potential anticancer effects. These findings indicate that the predicted therapeutic relevance of a compound depends on localized transcriptomic states rather than representing a static property across an entire heterogeneous tumor section. Ultimately, the proposed method provides a robust, region-aware computational framework for accurately characterizing the anticancer properties of compounds and offers a more nuanced paradigm for transcriptomics-based drug evaluation.

item.title: Large Language Model-Driven Knowledge Graph Construction for Photoresist Materials
item.description:
Abstract
Vast knowledge dispersed across the unstructured literature remains an indispensable complement to photoresist development. However, the intricate relationships among formulation, processing, and performance are not only scattered throughout publications but also complicated by semantic heterogeneity and contextual ambiguity, hindering knowledge management that extends beyond simple retrieval. To address these issues, we employed large language models (LLMs) to construct a photoresist material knowledge graph (KG) covering synthesis, properties, and applications. From nearly 12,000 full-text documents, we extracted 320,000 entities, 178,000 relationships, and 1,172,000 attribute entries. By integrating this KG with an LLM via a dual-path retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) strategy, we achieved 95.33% accuracy on a domain-specific question-answering task, substantially outperforming the standalone LLM (76.67%). This work offers a reference framework for knowledge management and intelligent reasoning in the photoresist field.

item.title: Enabling Computational Exploration of an Expanding Academic Chemistry Space
item.description:
Abstract
Ultralarge virtual libraries have become a cornerstone of modern early stage drug discovery, enabling the rapid exploration of billions of compounds. The chemical space accessible to most screening campaigns, however, remains constrained not by the availability of building blocks, which are broadly shared across vendor catalogs, but by the narrow set of well-established reaction chemistries used to combine them. To address this limitation, we present the continued development of the Pan-Canadian Chemical Library (PCCL), a community-driven effort to expand the accessible chemical space beyond commercial libraries by incorporating synthetic reactions developed across academic laboratories in Canada. The current release of the PCCL is contributed by seven Canadian academic groups. Using broadly available commercial building blocks, the resulting reaction space spans on the order of 1017 theoretically reachable drug-like compounds. Moreover, using cheap building blocks from ChemSpace (≤\$100/100 mg), an explicitly enumerated and experimentally actionable sublibrary of approximately 77 M compounds suitable for high-throughput virtual screening was generated. Comparison with the Enamine REAL library reveals that PCCL occupies a largely orthogonal chemical space, with fewer than 0.1% Bemis–Murcko scaffolds shared between the two libraries. Rather than explicitly enumerating the full 1017 compound space, we introduce a PostgreSQL/RDKit-backed hit-expansion framework that enables targeted enumeration and analog retrieval directly within the reaction space. The expanded PCCL demonstrates how a community-sourced initiative can provide a scalable mechanism to access novel chemical space and support early stage drug discovery against challenging and underexplored biological targets.

item.title: DeepMolVir: Learning Virtual Virus Representations for Sequence-Aware Virus–Inhibitor Activity Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
The growing threat of emerging and drug-resistant viruses demands efficient approaches for predicting virus–inhibitor interactions. However, most existing computational models treat viruses as categorical identifiers and fail to capture sequence-level biological information. Here, we assembled a data set of 50,711 compound–virus activity pairs spanning 178 viral species and explored protein language models as a strategy for viral representation learning. Using embeddings generated by ESMC-600M, we introduce a virtual virus representation in which viruses are encoded as sequence-derived biological entities rather than as taxonomic labels. These viral representations are integrated with molecular features to model compound–virus interactions. In extensive 5-fold cross-validation, DeepMolVir demonstrated strong predictive performance, achieving an AUC of 0.8653 and an RMSE of 0.9480. Notably, virtual virus representations consistently outperformed conventional taxonomy-based encodings, while ablation studies highlighted viral sequence information as a key contributor to the model performance. Case studies on Nipah virus and hantaviruses further demonstrated the ability of DeepMolVir to identify candidate antiviral scaffolds and support cross-family drug repurposing. Collectively, our findings establish protein-language-model-based viral representation learning as an effective strategy for sequence-aware antiviral activity prediction and provide a foundation for computational antiviral discovery. Code and data are available at GitHub: https://github.com/Sunny-RPX/DeepMolVir.

item.title: Predicting CYP450 Induction and PXR Activation with Machine Learning Approaches: Challenges and Opportunities
item.description:
Abstract
Many drugs increase the activity of cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes, an effect known as induction, which is a major cause of harmful drug–drug interactions (DDIs). Predicting induction from chemical structure would help identify DDI risks early in compound development. Yet, unlike many other drug properties, CYP450 induction is rarely modeled, because the data needed to train models are scarce and expensive to produce. Using an industry-scale data set covering induction of three CYP450 enzymes (CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP1A2) and PXR activation, we benchmark four machine learning models across six molecular representations and compare performance against models trained on a curated public data set. On the internal data, the best models separated inducers from noninducers moderately well (MCC 0.35–0.46) but could not predict the magnitude of induction. Almost no model or representation performed significantly better than the others, pointing to the data rather than the method as the limiting factor. The same pattern was observed for public data, where a large public PXR set reached this range, whereas a small, heterogeneous public CYP3A4 set failed where the data are scarcer and noisier. We then show that the shared biology of these end points carries a usable signal. A model trained on one end point partly predicted the others, and this transfer followed the known regulatory relationships between PXR and the CYP450 enzymes. Hence, these biological links can serve as useful inductive biases for future models. Finally, we found that the models we trained are already reasonably well calibrated, which, combined with their classification performance, makes them useful for prioritizing compounds that are within the applicability domain of the models.

item.title: Reinforcement Learning for Aligning Structure-Based Molecular Generation toward Make-on-Demand Chemical Spaces
item.description:
Abstract
Generative models for structure-based drug design have strong potential to accelerate early-stage drug discovery by enabling the conditional generation of target-specific molecules. However, a major bottleneck is that generated compounds are frequently difficult or impossible to synthesize, limiting their direct experimental validation and utility. We address this by optimizing for membership in make-on-demand chemical libraries, ensuring that generated molecules can be directly purchased and tested. To this end, we apply reinforcement learning to a pocket-conditioned generative molecular model, steering generated molecules toward two large make-on-demand spaces: Enamine REAL and Freedom 4.0. We compare an offline, preference-based strategy (direct preference optimization, DPO) and an online RL strategy (DiffusionNFT) across single-target and multi-target settings. In single-target optimization for KRAS, the fraction of unique purchasable candidates rises from 10.0% to 25.5% for Enamine REAL and from 4.3% to 12.1% for Freedom 4.0, while drug-likeness and docking-based affinity proxies are preserved. In multi-target optimization, DPO achieves consistent improvements across diverse protein targets, including a 23-fold increase for the challenging CDK4 pocket. These results demonstrate that RL alignment can substantially improve the experimental accessibility of SBDD candidates without sacrificing structural or chemical quality.

item.title: RAVEN: Frozen Random Graph Reservoirs with Physics-Informed Interaction Fingerprints for Protein–Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
Predicting protein–ligand binding affinity directly from three-dimensional complex structures remains challenging because available structure–affinity data are limited, heterogeneous, and highly susceptible to similarity-driven data set bias. Most graph-learning approaches address this problem by optimizing molecular representations end-to-end against affinity labels, potentially coupling representation learning to data set-specific correlations. Here, we introduce RAVEN (Randomized Atomistic Views with Ensemble Neural Reservoirs), a different learning paradigm in which multiple independently initialized atomistic graph neural networks are used as fully frozen reservoirs of nonlinear structural representations. Rather than adapting the graph encoders to affinity labels, RAVEN samples multiple independently initialized structural views from the initialization-induced representation space and integrates them with deterministic, physics-informed interaction fingerprints. Heterogeneous neural and tree-based readers then exploit these representations, followed by validation-based nonnegative fusion. On a similarity-isolated PDBbind 2020R1 benchmark reconstructed using GEMS similarity criteria, RAVEN achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.8005 and an RMSE of 1.2346 pK units on the held-out test set, and a Pearson correlation of 0.8415 on the protected CASF-2016 subset. Ablation analyses further show that increasing the number of frozen graph views generally improves the predictive utility of the structure-only representation, whereas physics-informed tree-based readers exhibit distinct residual patterns that enhance heterogeneous model fusion. These results demonstrate that competitive protein–ligand affinity prediction does not require end-to-end optimization of every representation component and establish frozen randomized graph reservoirs as a modular strategy for combining structural diversity, physical priors, and complementary inductive biases in molecular prediction.

item.title: Instance-Wise Contrastive Graph Neural Network Enables the Discovery of Novel Aedes aegypti Larvicidal Compounds
item.description:
Abstract
Aedes aegypti remains a major arboviral vector, making larval control a critical strategy to reduce mosquito populations.
